title: ES 'with witnesses' certificate format and an independent checker
connection: Standardised certificate (p, x, y, z) plus type metadata ↔ verification hygiene for all experiments.
why: Prevents silent errors in large censuses; trivial but useful infrastructure.
first_step: Write scripts/es_check_cert.py verifying 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) with exact integers and classifying Type I/II.

title: ES certificates for record-size Mordell-hard primes (Proth/generalised Fermat primes in square classes mod 840)
connection: Find a known huge prime p (≥ 10⁵ digits) in a Mordell-hard class and search small certificates (4uC−1) | p + u by trial division ↔ ES verified at a 'random' gigantic prime.
why: Cheap, publicity-friendly, and an adversarial data point at astronomically large p (does a small certificate always exist? the model predicts ≍ log² p ≈ 10¹¹ certificates but small ones are what is cheap to find).
first_step: Take primes from the Top-20 Proth list, reduce mod 840 to find one in a hard class, and run trial division of p + u by 4uC − 1 for uC ≤ 10⁶ using GMP.

title: Universal vs per-prime certificate menus: minimal menu covering all primes in [X, 2X]
connection: Set cover over a dyadic block ↔ how menu size must grow with X (B1 says unbounded).
why: The growth law of the minimal menu (e.g. ~ log X or ~ (log X)²) is a quantitative replacement for the qualitative B1 and could be compared with the CRT-adversary cost.
first_step: Greedy set cover for primes ≡ 1 mod 24 in [10^k, 2·10^k], k = 4..8, with menu items = (u,C) pairs; fit menu size vs k.

title: OEIS search: numbers not of the form tuv − u − v (t,u,v ≥ 2) and with 4 | t — is the sequence in OEIS?
connection: U(n)'s failure set (odd squares + {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}) is an explicit sequence; if it (or its variants) appears in OEIS, cross-references may reveal an independent characterisation.
why: OEIS cross-links occasionally reveal a known theorem behind a computed list.
first_step: Query OEIS for 105, 2961, 3985, 25305 and for the 14 (★) failure primes (409, …, 8813281).

title: OEIS A005097 (odd primes − 1)/2 ↔ numbers not of form 2xy + x + y: the bilinear primality template
connection: n ≠ 2xy + x + y ⟺ 2n + 1 prime: the simplest 'trilinear-word ⟺ primality' dictionary. ES's (★) word is the level-4C version with a sign flip.
why: These dictionaries show which word forms detect primality (dead) and which can be universal (ES) — the sign/level flip is the difference.
first_step: Generalise: for the form t·xy − x − y with fixed t, characterise non-represented n via divisors of tn + 1 ≡ −1 mod t; tabulate t = 2..12.

title: Problem 310: sharp dependence as finite-search bound
connection: Problem 310 ↔ ES F04, F12, F21, F23: bounded representation count, pointwise search and computational verification.
why: Sharp quantitative bounds can make a finite search meaningful by bounding the denominator range rather than merely checking arbitrary cutoffs.
first_step: Translate the Liu–Sawhney parameter bound into an explicit maximum denominator and compare with existing verified ES computation ranges.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0241] Extract the sharp dependence stated on the page; compare it to known computational ES denominator sizes as p grows.

title: Uniquely represented trilinear integers as a model for witness multiplicity
connection: OEIS A093669/A093670, cross-referenced by A025052, classify numbers with a unique representation by ab+ac+bc. They share F04/F13/F14: count integral points on a symmetric cubic-form fibre, including unusually sparse one-witness fibres.
why: ES work often needs a pointwise lower bound on representation counts; the neighboring exact-one locus is a useful benchmark for how divisor factorizations control multiplicity.
first_step: For primes p, compare the number of ordered ES solutions up to permutation with the analogous factorization count on a small trilinear surface; look for a divisor-sum identity or a stable multiplicity statistic.

title: Stern primes and a second notion of additive nonrepresentation
connection: The A060003 comments identify several small exceptions as odd Stern primes, i.e. primes not of the form p+2b². This combines prime inputs with a restricted additive representation and finite exceptional values, matching F01p/F10/F25/F29.
why: Separating prime inputs from composite exceptions might reveal whether ES prime witnesses are governed by a different density or local obstruction than composite n.
first_step: Run the same candidate-generation code on ES primes and composites separately, comparing first-witness distributions and residue classes with the Stern-prime subset in A060003.

title: Large gaps between detected representations and exceptional candidates
connection: A060003 reports progressively improved lower bounds for the next possible omitted value, with no claim that the sequence is complete. This matches F23/F24/F25/F32: computation, heuristic finiteness, explicit exceptions, and verifiable search bounds.
why: Its cautious treatment of a finite-looking sequence is a model for how to use extensive ES computation without mistaking a cutoff for a theorem.
first_step: For ES, record the largest tested prime and the exact complete divisor-search bound alongside every ‘no counterexample’ statement; do not report a cutoff without the bound proof.

title: Denominator-sum generating sequence for reciprocal representations
connection: The MO answer points to OEIS A051907, counting representations of 1 as unit fractions with a fixed denominator sum. This shares F04/F12/F19/F21: a coefficient/counting viewpoint turns reciprocal solutions into sequence coefficients indexed by a complexity statistic.
why: Generating-function and dynamic-programming methods can offer an independent way to enumerate restricted ES witnesses and compare expected counts.
first_step: Inspect A051907's definition and recurrence, then formulate the corresponding generating series for ordered ES triples by denominator sum or maximum denominator and compare low coefficients.

title: Strictly ordered cubic-form representations and symmetry reduction
connection: OEIS A093669 counts unique representations by ab+ac+bc under 0<a<b<c, removing permutation symmetry. It shares F04/F13/F14: a symmetric three-variable surface whose raw point count is converted to canonical unordered witnesses.
why: ES's S3 symmetry creates overcounting; the ordered-triple convention in this sequence offers an exact and transparent normalization.
first_step: For primes p, count only x≤y≤z ES triples and compare with the fully ordered count, separately tracking repeated-coordinate strata.

title: Unique-representation locus as a low-multiplicity test
connection: A093669 lists integers with exactly one strictly ordered representation as ab+ac+bc, sharing F04/F13/F25 and contrasting ES's expected polylogarithmic abundance with a rigid one-point fibre.
why: A unique-witness locus is a sensitive place to test whether an ES construction proves mere existence or can force multiple genuinely distinct solution orbits.
first_step: Enumerate ES primes with exactly one unordered solution orbit up to a modest cutoff and compare their factorization and residue signatures to the one-representation trilinear terms.

title: Factor-pair enumeration for a unique cubic-form witness
connection: A093669 provides a computation for unique ab+ac+bc representations by looping over a,b and testing whether n−ab is divisible by a+b, yielding c. This matches F10/F15/F32: each fibre is reduced to a divisor/congruence test and can be exhaustively certified.
why: It is a low-cost exact enumeration architecture analogous to fixed-variable ES hyperbola factorization, and can validate a new ES candidate-family search.
first_step: Implement the A093669 loop pattern for ES after fixing one denominator, using the exact split-hyperbola divisor condition; compare outputs against independent brute force for small p.

title: Addition chains: certificate search with rigorous lower bounds
connection: Addition chains match ES through F01,F32,F23,F24: finite verifiable certificates, computer searches, and a global existence/bound problem. The Scholz–Brauer problem also illustrates the gap between finding certificates and proving optimality.
why: ES witnesses are NP-style certificates; addition-chain exact-search methods could improve reproducible bounded ES searches and expose hard residue classes.
first_step: Build a bounded-depth ES certificate enumerator that canonicalizes symmetric triples and records the first uncovered prime at each depth.

title: Computational proof certificates for Diophantine existence
connection: Certificate problems share F23, F32, F35: a compact witness is easy to verify even when finding one universally is hard.
why: A verifiable finite certificate could support modular reductions or proof-carrying searches over residue classes.
first_step: Design a checker for a residue-class identity certificate and verify its proof obligations independently of the generator.

title: Certificate-length bounds and NP-style arithmetic witnesses
connection: Small-witness problems share F32, F01, F23: every positive instance has a short certificate even if universal existence is open.
why: Uniform certificate bounds can make exhaustive search on reduced instances feasible and enable proof-carrying transformations.
first_step: Derive an explicit bound on the minimal ES denominator from known constructions and test whether it is polynomial in p with effective constants.

title: Salez's modular filters (verification to 10¹⁷) as an explicit infinite covering family
connection: Salez found new modular equations (identity families) and used them as sieving filters to verify ES to 10¹⁷ (F23, F03, F34).
why: The filters are a concrete enumerated set of 'lines'; their combined density deficit as a function of the number of filters is an explicit covering-rate curve to compare with the Poisson model.
first_step: Extract Salez's filter list and compute the density of primes left uncovered by the first k filters for k up to 10³; fit the decay rate.

title: Mihnea & Bogdan (arXiv 2509.00128, 2025): ES verified to 10¹⁸ with solution-count data f(p) — data for signature calibration
connection: The paper extends verification to 10¹⁸ and evaluates the solution-counting function f(p) (F23, F04); check what count statistics are reported.
why: Independent count data to calibrate the log²p model against an outside source.
first_step: Compare their reported count statistics with M_BM(p) predictions at matching heights.

title: Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang sunflowers among minimal ES solutions → identity families
connection: ALWZ improved sunflower bounds to (log w)^{w(1+o(1))}; families of ES solutions across many n, encoded as sets of prime-power factors of (x,y,z), contain sunflowers, which correspond to shared 'cores' i.e. parametric identity families.
why: Mechanically extracts polynomial identities (Mordell-type) from solution data.
first_step: Encode the minimal solutions for primes p ≤ 10^6 in a fixed Mordell class as sets of (prime, exponent, slot) and search for sunflowers with ≥3 petals.
refs: Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang, Improved bounds for the sunflower lemma, Ann. Math. 194 (2021), arXiv:1908.08483

title: Fargues–Scholze / local Langlands — no natural ES object (recorded)
connection: Geometrisation of local Langlands (Fargues–Scholze) concerns representations of p-adic groups; ES has no evident reductive-group or Galois-representation object attached.
why: Recording the null result prevents later re-proposal; the nearest real link would go through automorphic forms attached to ES counts (theta series), which are GL₂/GL₁ and need no geometrisation.
first_step: Ask whether any ES count is a Fourier coefficient of an automorphic form on a group of rank ≥ 2; if not, close.
refs: Fargues–Scholze, Geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence, arXiv:2102.13459

title: ECM/GNFS-free certificate search: choose C so 4Cp+1 is smooth-friendly
connection: Certificate search is bottlenecked by factoring p-tied integers; ES only needs some divisor in a class, so partial factorisation (ECM to bound B) suffices for most C.
why: Practical speed-up for adversarial searches beyond 10^25, giving better 'hardest prime' calibration data.
first_step: Measure on hard primes the fraction of certificates found using only ECM with B1 = 10^4 on the first X slices; estimate cost per certificate.
refs: Lenstra, Factoring integers with elliptic curves, Ann. Math. 126 (1987)

title: Harvey–van der Hoeven O(n log n) multiplication / fast sieving for verification beyond 10^18
connection: Asymptotically optimal integer multiplication and modern segmented sieving speed up the ES verification pipeline (Salez 10^17, Mihnea–Dumitru 10^18).
why: Extending verification is calibration only, but cheap engineering improvements shift the 'explicit range' needed by any analytic tail.
first_step: Profile the repo's verify.py on a 10^9 block at 10^18 and identify whether multiplication, sieving, or modular inversion dominates.
refs: Harvey–van der Hoeven, Integer multiplication in time O(n log n), Ann. Math. 193 (2021)

title: Distributed GPU search for counterexamples in Mordell-hard cells beyond 10^18 (targeted, not exhaustive)
connection: Exhaustive verification is at 10^18; targeted search in the lowest-count residue cells (DISPROOF_AVENUES) at 10^20–10^30 is feasible on GPUs with Type II e-slice tests.
why: Calibration of the zero law at much larger scales where expected counts are still polylog.
first_step: Port the e-slice test to CUDA for a fixed cell and benchmark primes per second at 10^24.

title: Persistent data releases + OEIS-style sequence mining for ES statistics
connection: Many breakthroughs came from noticing sequences (OEIS); ES statistics (min-count primes, record-hard primes, sibling failure lists) could be matched against OEIS.
why: Cheap: an OEIS hit could connect ES failure sets of siblings to known sequences (e.g. S_{n,−4} failures {2,9,21,165,945,1197}).
first_step: Query OEIS for the sibling failure lists and U(n)'s sporadic set {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}.

title: OAI 138 Subset Sum in 2^{0.49n} (claimed) — e-slice as subset-product search
connection: e-slice success is a subset-product problem: choose a sub-multiset of prime factors of N whose product ratio is −1 mod e; with ω(N) small, brute force is trivial, but for highly composite N or pooled factors it's subset-sum in ℤ/(e−1) (discrete logs).
why: Fast subset-sum algorithms matter only if one pools many factors (e.g. across slices) — a computational lens on pooled certificates.
first_step: Estimate typical ω(N) at slices; if pooled designs push it past ~40, benchmark meet-in-the-middle subset-product search.

title: Lenstra integer programming in fixed dimension for 'certificate in a box' decisions
connection: Lenstra/Kannan: integer feasibility in fixed dimension is polynomial; certificate existence with bounded parameters is a low-dimensional integer program with a divisibility constraint (non-linear).
why: Linearising divisibility via auxiliary variables gives an IP; feasibility algorithms could replace factoring in searches.
first_step: Model 'f·g = 4Cp+1, f ≡ −1 (4C), C ≤ X' as a quadratic IP and test whether branch-and-bound beats factoring at p ~ 10^20.
refs: Lenstra, Integer programming with a fixed number of variables, Math. Oper. Res. 8 (1983)

title: PARI/Magma class-field computations: explicit 'ES ray class fields' for small (c,d)
connection: Computer algebra computes ray class fields explicitly; ES Type I certificates for fixed (c,d) correspond to primes f splitting in a specific ray class field with a twist by p.
why: Explicit fields allow Chebotarev-density computations of the per-(c,d) success probability, sharpening M_BM.
first_step: Compute with PARI bnrinit for d ≤ 10, c ≤ 5 and list Frobenius conditions.

title: OEIS / experimental-math lookup of ES-derived sequences
connection: Sequences such as λ(p), least certificate level, N₋(p), I3_𝒞 least u, the U(n) failure list and the ES₅ failure list. Lookups in OEIS and the Inverse Symbolic Calculator may connect them to unrelated known sequences.
why: It is cheap, native to experimental mathematics, and occasionally finds hidden identities (e.g. a match with a class-number sequence).
first_step: Compute the first 50 terms of 6 derived sequences and search OEIS; record hits.

title: Integer-relation search (PSLQ/LLL) for N₋(p) or the slot-count in a basis of arithmetic functions
connection: Try to express N₋(p), N₊(p) or the ES₅ word count as an integer combination of standard arithmetic functions of p and p-tied integers (τ(p+k), class numbers h(−kp), r₂, r₃(kp), …).
why: A found identity is a candidate exact formula (an R-type rigidity). A null result over a large basis is evidence against simple formulas. SIGN_IDENTITY did a version; the basis can be widened.
first_step: Build a basis of 200 functions evaluated at 2000 primes; run integer relation detection (LLL on the evaluation matrix) for N₋(p).

title: Elkies-style 'search for structure' in large-height ES solutions via lattice reduction
connection: Elkies's ABC/Euler-conjecture searches use lattice reduction to find large solutions with structure. For ES, solutions with exceptionally large minimal x (hardest p) might be found by targeted lattice search, giving data on 'how hard' primes look.
why: It is the computational-NT native way to probe extreme cases, giving better test cases than random primes.
first_step: Search primes p < 10¹⁵ near pseudosquares for the maximal least-certificate level using lattice-guided sampling; record extremes.

title: Kernel-checked verification tables (Lean/Coq certificates) for ES up to large bounds
connection: Store per-prime certificates (x,y,z) or compact Type I/II data and verify them inside a proof assistant (by computation via norm_num/decide or a verified checker).
why: Infrastructure: a formal ES-up-to-N theorem makes formal T1, slot lemma and the reductions usable together with numeric bounds. It is cheap relative to its reuse value.
first_step: Prototype: verify ES for p < 10⁶ in Lean 4 from a certificate file with a verified checker; measure time.

title: Escalation of certificate menus: the ES 'truant' tree
connection: Bhargava's escalation: adjoin the smallest truant each time; finitely many escalators. ES: start with a certificate menu (Mordell identities, (★), b=1, ES₅, windows), find the least prime not covered, adjoin the cheapest family covering it, iterate; study the growth of the escalation tree.
why: Gives an empirical picture of how many families are needed up to X (B1 says bounded menus fail under Hypothesis H — the escalation rate measures how fast menus must grow).
first_step: Implement escalation over the repo's family menu up to 10⁸ and plot menu size vs. X.

title: Prime-factor census by CRT: q | 4Cp+1 iff C ≡ −(4p)⁻¹ (mod q)
connection: In Bertrand/Chebyshev the prime factorisation of a binomial coefficient is explicit. Here every prime q ∤ 2p divides 4Cp+1 exactly on one class C ≡ c_q (mod q); a single-prime certificate exists iff 4c_q | q+1 for some q ≡ 3 (mod 4) (C = c_q < q). Higher certificates combine several q's at a common C.
why: Makes the certificate problem an explicit combinatorial problem on the residues c_q(p); single-prime certificates have probability ≈ τ((q+1)/4)/q, summing to ≍ log²p — the main term in a transparent form.
first_step: Compute the single-prime-certificate count S₁(p) = #{q ≡ 3 (4) prime : 4c_q(p) | q+1} for p ≤ 10⁸ and its share of R(p); check whether S₁(p) alone ever vanishes for p in the hard list.

title: Smith-type distribution of 'certificate-free levels' in twist families
connection: Smith's method computes distributions of Selmer groups in quadratic-twist families. The set of levels C at which p has no certificate is a 'Selmer-like' local-global object varying with p; its distribution over p could be computed by Smith/Koymans–Pagano-style methods.
why: Exact distributional knowledge of the failing-level profile is stronger than the zero-law heuristics now used.
first_step: Define the profile vector (1[level C fails])_{C ≤ K} and tabulate its empirical distribution over p; compare with a product-of-local-factors model.

title: EGZ-style reduction: from 'composite' certificates to prime-level statements
connection: EGZ for n = ab follows from EGZ for a and b by iterated extraction. ES certificates at a level 4C = 4C₁C₂: is a certificate at level C obtainable from structure at levels C₁ and C₂ (e.g. a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C₁ and one ≡ −1 mod 4C₂ combined via CRT)?
why: If levels compose, it suffices to handle prime (power) levels, where character theory is simplest.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ test: when 4C₁p+1 and 4C₂p+1 have certificates, does 4C₁C₂p + 1 have one more often than chance?

title: Closure maps: certificate(p) ∧ certificate(q) ⇒ certificate(r) for some r(p,q)
connection: Wilson's PBD-closure and Graham's 2n+2/2n+9 maps produce 'every large n' from finitely many seeds. ES is closed under n → kn only; search for genuinely bilinear closure operations producing certificates for new primes r from certificates of p and q.
why: Any nontrivial closure operation on certificate-carrying primes would be a completely new structural fact about ES.
first_step: Brute-force search: for pairs of (★) triples (u₁,B₁,C₁), (u₂,B₂,C₂), test small bilinear/polynomial combinations for producing triples of other primes.

title: Minimum-modulus-type statement: every certificate system covering a class must use a small modulus
connection: Hough: every distinct covering has a modulus ≤ 10¹⁶. ES analogue: for each Mordell-hard class r mod 840, any finite set of (★) congruences covering all primes in r ∩ [X, 2X] must include moduli of a certain size or divisibility (e.g. divisible by many small primes). Gives structural information on what certificates must look like.
why: Constraints on the moduli of any covering are a form of 'forced structure' usable in a proof by contradiction.
first_step: Empirically compute, for each hard class and dyadic X, the greedy minimum set of moduli covering all primes; record its smallest modulus and prime-divisibility profile.
refs: arXiv:1307.0874 (Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. Math. 181 (2015))

title: Distribution of certificates across dyadic level ranges
connection: Primes in every short interval vs almost all: the analogue at fixed p is whether certificates appear in every dyadic level range [K, 2K] (K ≤ p^{1/2}) or cluster. With R(p) ≍ log²p spread over ≍ log p dyadic ranges, ≍ log p certificates per range are expected.
why: If every dyadic range typically carries certificates, a proof could target one range of convenient size (e.g. C ≈ p^{1/3}) where tools are best; if they cluster, that range is fixed by the data.
first_step: For p ≤ 10¹⁰ in the hard list, histogram certificates by ⌊log₂ C⌋ and record the empty ranges.

title: Ramanujan-type congruences for ES counts on progressions
connection: Ramanujan/Ono congruences say p(An + B) ≡ 0 (mod m). Search for progressions An + B on which f_II(n) or R(n) is always ≡ 0 (mod m) (m = 2, 3, 4, 8) beyond the trivial evenness; such congruences would reveal modular structure that might also produce nonzero congruences at primes.
why: Systematic congruence mining is cheap and has historically uncovered hidden modular structure.
first_step: Compute f_II(n), R(n) for n ≤ 10⁷ and test all A ≤ 840, B mod A for congruences mod 2, 3, 4, 8.
refs: Ono, Ann. Math. 151 (2000) 293-307 (Distribution of the partition function modulo m)

title: Eventual periodicity of 'ES-easy' residue structures (Wilson-style)
connection: Wilson showed the set of orders admitting designs is eventually periodic, so finitely many residue classes need checking. For ES sub-routes, test whether 'the set of levels C at which the BM main term is positive for all p in a class r mod M' is eventually periodic in C, giving a finite description of guaranteed-positive levels.
why: Eventually periodic structures can be checked by finite computation and then fed into an every-p argument.
first_step: For M = 840, compute for each hard class r the set of C ≤ 10⁴ with M_C^lev > 0 for all p ≡ r (mod M·4C) and test periodicity in C.

title: Uncovered density of the (★) system restricted to moduli with bounded prime factors
connection: Hough's argument tracks how the uncovered set shrinks as primes are added to the moduli. Restrict ES congruences p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) to moduli 4uB built from primes ≤ y; compute the uncovered density δ(y) among integers in the hard classes and its decay in y.
why: A precise decay law for δ(y) (power of log y? exp?) quantifies how many prime 'layers' certificates need — a structural fingerprint of ES.
first_step: Compute δ(y) for y ≤ 50 by inclusion over moduli dividing a bounded smooth number, restricted to n ≤ 10⁸ in hard classes.
refs: arXiv:1307.0874 (Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. Math. 181 (2015))

title: Hardest residue cases needed new constructions: identify ES's 'case 3 mod 12'
connection: In Ringel–Youngs some residue classes (e.g. cases 1, 9 mod 12) took years and ad hoc ideas. Among the six Mordell-hard classes mod 840 (1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529), measure which is hardest (lowest counts, most sub-route failures) and focus constructions there.
why: Concentrating effort on the hardest class mirrors the historical endgame.
first_step: From census data, compute per-class mean/minimum of R(p)/log²p and sub-route failure counts.

title: Sign/size arguments on special values: choose auxiliary objects whose values have forced factors
connection: Elkies chose D so that H_D(j(E)) has a controlled sign and size. ES: choose auxiliary integers built from p (values of polynomials P(p) or norms from auxiliary fields) whose sign/size/Jacobi symbol forces a prime factor in a class tied to a level C, with the factor also dividing 4Cp + 1.
why: A systematic search space for 'forcing' constructions that guarantee prime factors in classes.
first_step: Search quadratic polynomials P with P(p) | (4Cp+1)·(something) for families of C and compute Jacobi-symbol constraints on their prime factors.

title: Multiplicative energy of divisor classes vs additive shifts N_e = (p + e)/4
connection: Sum-product: sets with small multiplicative energy have large sumsets. The divisor-class multisets of N_e across consecutive windows e (an additive progression in N) — compute their multiplicative energies; ES failure across many windows would force large multiplicative structure (subgroup trapping) along an additive progression.
why: Quantitative version of the sum-product incompatibility item, measurable on data.
first_step: For hard primes, compute E^×(classes of divisors of N_e mod e) for e ≤ 10³ and compare with random integers.

title: Sun-style refinements as data: four-square-like refinements of ES
connection: Sun formulated many 'refined Lagrange' conjectures by computer search; several were proved. Generate ES refinements automatically (x + y or z constrained to be a square, a prime, ≡ r mod m, etc.), test them to 10⁷, and keep those that never fail — new conjectures whose extra structure may make them provable or reveal hidden symmetries.
why: Automated conjecture generation found provable statements for sums of squares; ES has never been mined this way systematically (check repo).
first_step: Write a search over ~200 refinement predicates P(x, y, z, p) and test on all p ≤ 10⁶; report survivors.
refs: arXiv:2003.02592 (Machiavelo-Tsopanidis, Zhi-Wei Sun's 1-3-5 conjecture and variations)

title: Erdős–Vaaler-type restricted versions: ES with levels restricted to squarefree or prime C
connection: Before Duffin–Schaeffer was proved in general, restricted cases (ψ supported on special sets) were proved first. Restrict ES (★) to prime levels C (or squarefree C): the overlap structure simplifies (gcd(C, C′) = 1). Study the prime-level-only (★) failure set and its overlap model.
why: Restricted versions with clean overlap structure are the natural first targets of a Duffin–Schaeffer-type method.
first_step: Compute (★) restricted to prime C for p ≤ 10⁹ and list failures; fit an independence model.

title: Positive proportion before density one (Bourgain–Fuchs) for bounded-shape certificates
connection: Bourgain–Fuchs proved a positive proportion of integers are Apollonian curvatures before density one. For ES, bounded-shape certificate families (u, B ≤ U fixed) cover a positive proportion of primes by Dirichlet; quantify the proportion covered by shapes with u, B ≤ U as U grows, versus the full ES density one.
why: Measures how much of ES is 'explained' by bounded shapes (Mordell-type) vs growing ones — the shape-growth rate needed for density one.
first_step: Compute coverage of primes ≤ 10⁹ by (★) with u, B ≤ U for U = 1..100.
refs: arXiv:2307.02749 (Haag-Kertzer-Rickards-Stange, The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false)

title: Third-method insurance: find a family whose success is uncorrelated with both (★) and b=1
connection: Holowinsky–Soundararajan needed exactly two complementary methods. ES data show (★) ∪ b=1 never fail together ≤ 10⁸, but a proof-grade argument may need a third family whose success correlates with neither (e.g. ES₅, Type I lines, small windows). Measure correlations of success indicators among 6–8 families.
why: Identifies the minimal robust family set for a complementary-methods proof.
first_step: Compute the correlation matrix of family success indicators (and of their counts) over primes ≤ 10⁸ in Mordell-hard classes.
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: Finite base + closure: what finite verification would an ES closure theorem need?
connection: Graham's 77-theorem needed a finite check (78–333) plus closure maps. If any closure/transfer system for ES certificates were found (see closure items), compute the minimal 'base' of verified instances it needs; ES is verified to 10¹⁸, so any closure system with base ≤ 10¹⁸ would finish.
why: Turns closure-map searches into a concrete success criterion.
first_step: For each candidate closure map found by search, compute the set of primes it reaches from primes ≤ 10⁶ and check whether its complement thins out.
refs: Graham, A theorem on partitions, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 3 (1963) 435-441 (77-theorem); see also Graham, Pacific J. Math. 10 (1960) 1221-1224 / OEIS A051882 (subagent dating conflict: check)

title: Limit objects of normalised divisor-class data as p → ∞ (Sendov's limiting measures)
connection: Tao's Sendov proof studies limiting zero distributions. For ES, attach to p the empirical measure of (log d / log N, class of d mod 4C) over levels C ≤ K and divisors d of 4Cp + 1; study its limit as p → ∞ (should be a product of uniform measures) and the rate; a counterexample sequence would converge to a measure avoiding a fixed 'certificate region'.
why: Gives a concrete limit object for compactness arguments.
first_step: Compute these empirical measures for p ~ 10⁶, 10⁸, 10¹⁰ and measure distance to the product-uniform model.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: Chain constraint x | y | z: fails at 38 of 269 primes below 4000
connection: 4/p = (1/x)(1 + 1/a + 1/(ab)) with y = ax, z = abx. The chain world is a 3-parameter subfamily; failures start at p = 73, 193, 313, 337.
why: Chain solutions correspond to Engel-type expansions; if chain failures are infinite but explained by a congruence, it shows how restrictive monotone (Engel/Sylvester-like) structure is.
first_step: (161 failures among 1125 primes below 2·10^4.) Characterize: x | y | z ⇔ p·(ab + b + 1) = 4abx; derive the congruence conditions on p and compare with the failure list.
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)

title: Engel and Pierce expansions: ES as a length-3 Engel-type representation
connection: Chain solutions (x | y | z) are Engel-like (1/x(1 + 1/a(1 + 1/b))). Engel/Pierce expansions of 4/n are deterministic; their lengths give a dynamical invariant.
why: If a variant of Engel expansion of 4/n always has length ≤ 3 after a single 'reset', ES follows; computing it is cheap.
first_step: Compute the Engel expansion length of 4/p for p ≤ 10^5; correlate with chain-world failures (38 below 4000).
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)

title: Integral fusion rings of rank 4 with Egyptian dimension equations (Alekseyev–Bruns–Dong)
connection: Classification of integral Grothendieck rings and modular data uses Egyptian-fraction equations with constraints, solved by computer to high rank. Their algorithms enumerate Egyptian solutions under divisibility constraints efficiently.
why: Their enumeration techniques (Bruns' Normaliz, divisibility pruning) could be reused for exhaustive constrained-ES censuses.
first_step: Read the algorithm sections of arXiv:2507.07023 and arXiv:2302.01613; assess reuse for ES censuses.

title: q-deformed rationals (Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko) and the continued-fraction form ES₅
connection: q-deformed rationals [a/b]_q are defined via continued fractions; ES₅ characterizes ES via continued-fraction length. A q-ES₅ statement could be stated for [4/p]_q and tested for positivity of coefficients.
why: q-rationals have total positivity and Jones-polynomial interpretations; a positivity statement for q-ES₅ might be provable and specialize at q = 1.
first_step: Check whether Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko 'q-deformed rationals and q-continued fractions' (Forum Math. Sigma 2020) defines sums; test [4/p]_q against sums of three q-unit fractions.

title: Fixed-length words in SL₂(ℤ): Waring problem for SL₂ / word maps
connection: Every element of SL₂(ℤ/p) is a product of ≤ 3 (or bounded) elements of a given type (Waring for word maps; Larsen–Shalev). ES₅ is a fixed-length word condition in SL₂(ℤ) with integrality.
why: Bounded-width results in finite groups are proved by character theory (Frobenius formula) — a 'thick' count over the group — but ES needs integral lifts.
first_step: Check whether the ES₅ word count over SL₂(ℤ/N) is given by a Frobenius character formula and whether lifting to ℤ is the only gap.

title: Bounded generation of SL₂(ℤ[1/p]) / elementary matrices (Carter–Keller, Vsemirnov)
connection: Bounded generation results (every matrix a product of ≤ N elementary matrices) are pointwise for every element, proved by arithmetic (Dirichlet's theorem) — closest to 'fixed-length word exists for every target'.
why: ES₅ is an existence of a fixed-length word; bounded generation proofs use primes in APs to steer entries.
first_step: Read Vsemirnov / Morgan–Rapinchuk–Sury on bounded generation of SL₂(ℤ[1/p]) and compare the word shape with ES₅'s.

title: t=1 and t=2 word counts are τ(n+1) and τ(2n+1) (OEIS A000005, A099774)
connection: The t=1 slice of tuv−u−v=n is (u−1)(v−1)=n+1 → τ(n+1); the t=2 slice is (2u−1)(2v−1)=2n+1 → τ(2n+1) (OEIS confirmed).
why: Sanity anchor for the word sieve, and a reminder that each t-slice is a divisor function of tn+1 restricted to −1 mod t — the 'tied-modulus divisor event'.
first_step: None (anchor); use as unit tests.

title: U(p) vs CF period of √p (ρ = −0.27)
connection: Longer CF period of √p (larger regulator) ⇒ fewer ES solutions.
why: ES has continued-fraction reformulations (ES₅, λ(p) ≤ 3); the CF of √p is a different object, but the correlation goes through L(1,χ_p) = 2hR/√p.
first_step: Partial correlation of U with CF period controlling for L(1,χ_p); if ≈ 0, the CF of √p carries nothing extra.

title: Continued fraction of 4/p and its partial quotients vs U(p)
connection: 4/p has a short CF; ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3 is about CF lengths of p/A for certain A. Correlate U(p) with the CF length/max partial quotient of p/A over small A.
why: Bridges the CF formulation (Zaremba-type, ZAREMBA_TRANSFER.md) to the count; a strong correlation would suggest Zaremba/Bourgain–Kontorovich density tools apply.
first_step: For each p compute #{A < p : CF length of p/A ≤ 3} (the five-slice count) and Spearman with U(p).

title: 105 is the unique non-square n ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ killing all three word families
connection: R(105) = Uv(105) = I3(105) = 0 and ESC(105) = 0; every other non-square n ≡ 1 (4) has at least two families alive.
why: 105 = 3·5·7 is 'locally square' modulo 8 and small primes? (105 ≡ 1 mod 8, 105 ≡ 0 mod 3,5,7) — its divisibility by 3,5,7 kills shifts; a structural characterisation would explain uniqueness.
first_step: Check whether n = 3·5·7·m² or other 'n ≡ 0 mod 105' families have systematically few words.

title: Divisor-chain x | y never fails (all primes ≤ 10⁵, all n ≤ 3000)
connection: Every n in range has an ES solution with x | y (share 0.14 of solutions); 4/n − 1/z = (k+1)/(kx) means 4/n − 1/z = a/b (lowest terms) with b having a divisor ≡ −1 (mod a).
why: x | y is the 'divisor ≡ −1 (mod a)' event again — equivalent in spirit to the word families (tuv − u − v); a direct bridge between the Egyptian-fraction shape and the word/U formulation.
first_step: Write the bijection between x | y solutions and words n = tuv − u − v (or a sub-family) and compare counts.

title: Distinct-only count D(p) = U(p) at p ≡ 1 (4); U(p) − D(p) = 2 exactly at every prime p ≡ 3 (4), p > 7
connection: Verified over all primes ≤ 2·10⁵: U − D = 0 at all 8 977 primes ≡ 1 (4) and U − D = 2 at all 9 004 primes ≡ 3 (4) > 7 — the two isosceles solutions predicted by the factorisations (4x−2p)(4z−p) = 2p² and (4x−p)(4z−2p) = 2p².
why: Exact corollary of the proved isosceles law: the distinct and non-distinct ES problems coincide on the hard class, and the orbit-size correction O(p) − 6D(p) is an explicit constant at p ≡ 3 (4).
first_step: Write as a corollary next to the isosceles lemma; the orbit formula O(p) = 6U(p) − 6 (p ≡ 3 mod 4), O(p) = 6U(p) (p ≡ 1 mod 4) holds at every prime 2·10⁴–2·10⁵ (checked); see whether A292624 states it.

title: A287116 (Alekseyev): non-square n not of the form 4M − d with ab | M, d | a+b: only 288, 336, 4545 below 2·10⁹
connection: Dubickas–Novikas' set E(4) formulation; our ESC zero set (no word coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − n)) contains 288 and 336 too (plus 105, 672, 1380, …), but not 4545.
why: Two different word-type certificate systems share the exceptional values 288 and 336; A287116's finiteness would imply ES (entry comment). Mapping our families onto the 4M − d form unifies the campaign's word families with Dubickas–Novikas.
first_step: Check ESC(4545) and the A287116 condition at 105, 672, 1380; write the explicit dictionary between (t,u,v) words and (M,a,b,d).
refs: Dubickas–Novikas, Acta Math. Univ. Comenianae 81(2), 2012 (as cited by OEIS A287116; https://www.iam.fmph.uniba.sk/amuc/_vol-81/_no_2/_dubickas/dubickas.html — check)

title: Moving the first denominator
connection: Connect changes x→x+1 with changes in the residual factor-pair problem, treating consecutive x as coupled rather than independent trials.
why: Neighboring residual numerators differ by four, so their divisor searches share arithmetic structure.
first_step: Tabulate success transitions between neighboring x for 100 primes.

title: Cluster-style mutations
connection: Search for involutions on auxiliary ES parametrizations analogous to replacing one root of a quadratic while fixing other variables.
why: An exact positive integral mutation could propagate certificates across a connected graph.
first_step: For three existing elementary parametrizations, solve for each coordinate and test whether another integral branch exists.

title: Trace identities in SL₂
connection: Connect two-by-two matrix trace identities with the campaign's word formulations and seek trace-preserving congruence moves.
why: Matrix words package nonlinear integer expressions into exact multiplication laws.
first_step: Derive the trace relation for three short elementary matrices and compare it with tuv−u−v.

title: Continued-fraction surgery
connection: Study local replacements in continued fractions that change a certificate's congruence data without making its length too large.
why: Equivalent rational expansions can trade coefficient signs, sizes, and parity.
first_step: Enumerate short continued-fraction identities and label which preserve positivity and desired coefficient classes.

title: Continuants modulo powers of two
connection: Analyze short continuant recurrences modulo 8,16,32 and compare reachable states with the admissible coordinate classes.
why: Finite parity information may guide an otherwise unbounded integer construction.
first_step: Build the exact transition graph for continuants modulo 16 with coefficient residues as labels.

title: Euclidean quotient parity
connection: Track parity of Euclidean quotients together with remainder size when processing p and an auxiliary parameter.
why: Parity-decorated Euclidean descent could interact with the required classes modulo four.
first_step: Compute quotient-parity strings for certificates found by a fixed divisor search and compare with controls.

title: Semigroup holes
connection: Treat attainable certificate parameters under positive identity composition as an affine semigroup and inspect its holes.
why: Eventual saturation is a meaningful possibility even when small exceptions persist.
first_step: Generate the semigroup from a small set of verified composition moves and compute missing points in a bounded region.

title: Torus rotations for denominator rounding
connection: Express the rounding error of p divided by a small parameter as a fractional-part coordinate.
why: Related rotations may coordinate two rounding choices whose errors must cancel.
first_step: Derive the exact residual after two floor-based denominator choices and plot the error pair.

title: Flow networks for factor allocation
connection: Model allocation of prime-power factors to denominator components as a capacitated network when the valuation constraints permit it.
why: Flow feasibility can solve the allocation part exactly, leaving residue constraints visible.
first_step: For a factored small auxiliary integer, derive factor capacities and compare feasible flows with actual certificates.

title: Regular languages of valid matrix words
connection: Describe congruence-admissible matrix words by a finite automaton and distinguish this from their unbounded integer values.
why: Congruence admissibility is genuinely finite-state, providing a rigorous symbolic skeleton.
first_step: Build an automaton for elementary matrices modulo 8 with accepting states matching one required coordinate condition.

title: Markov bases for certificate fibers
connection: Seek finite move sets connecting all nonnegative solutions of a fixed linearized parameter constraint.
why: Connectivity of the linear fiber could reduce enumeration before nonlinear conditions are imposed.
first_step: Compute a kernel basis for a toy exponent-allocation matrix and test which moves preserve positivity.

title: Lax-pair discovery as an algebraic search
connection: Ask whether a certificate-preserving transformation admits a matrix conjugation description with invariant characteristic polynomial.
why: A Lax representation would expose conserved quantities, not by itself guarantee positive integer orbits.
first_step: For one verified rational map, search two-by-two matrix entries of low degree satisfying the conjugation equation.

title: Symplectic coordinates for matrix words
connection: Use the area-preserving action of SL₂ on pairs of coordinates to track certificate-related invariants.
why: An invariant determinant can constrain possible moves more cleanly than expanded polynomials.
first_step: Choose two column vectors from a short word and compute which parameter changes preserve their determinant and residue labels.

title: Modular geodesic coding
connection: Compare continued-fraction certificate words with symbolic codes of geodesic segments on the modular surface.
why: Geometric coding may organize word length and cusp excursions, while the ES condition remains arithmetic.
first_step: Translate several short certificate words into matrices and compute their fixed points and trace types.

title: Horocycle sampling of congruence states
connection: Study elementary unipotent matrix orbits modulo small integers and their integer-height growth.
why: These are explicit orbits that could generate systematic candidate families.
first_step: Enumerate products of two unipotent flows modulo 16 and track the least integer height realizing each target state.

title: Homogeneous-flow shrinking targets
connection: Rephrase finding short lattice vectors with extra congruences as a target-hitting problem in a family of lattices.
why: The formulation may identify what effective recurrence statement would suffice.
first_step: Write the exact target region for one lattice encoding and calculate how its volume changes with p.

title: Skew products coupling size and residue
connection: Track a real size coordinate together with a finite residue state under a certificate-related recurrence.
why: This separates growth from arithmetic admissibility while keeping their interaction explicit.
first_step: Build the skew-product map for a short Euclidean or matrix recurrence and plot admissible returns.

title: Interval-exchange selectors
connection: Use interval maps associated with rational approximation to partition parameter choices into symbolic regimes.
why: A finite partition might yield a small list of exact denominator formulas on each regime.
first_step: Compute return itineraries for a simple interval map and test whether an exact residual formula is constant in symbolic type.

title: Periodic-orbit certificate families
connection: Search for parameter recurrences with periodic residue states and nonperiodic integer growth.
why: A periodic modular pattern can preserve admissibility along an infinite arithmetic orbit.
first_step: For one exact recurrence, enumerate cycles modulo 8 and verify which lifted initial points remain positive integers.

title: Return-time distributions
connection: Measure first visits to admissible residue states in deterministic certificate-generating dynamics.
why: Return-time tails are directly connected to the cost of the resulting search procedure.
first_step: For several initial states, record first-hit times and compare them with orbit component sizes.

title: Arithmetic cocycles
connection: Record a multiplicative scale factor and a congruence correction along each matrix or continued-fraction move.
why: The cocycle may reveal telescoping products that enforce integrality after a whole word.
first_step: Compute the scale cocycle for three verified moves and search short loops with unit total correction.

title: Embeddings of matrix words
connection: Learn or hand-design representations that place equivalent or easily transformable matrix words near each other.
why: A useful representation could guide discovery of short exact rewrite sequences.
first_step: Compare embeddings based on modular actions with raw word edit distance on verified equivalent words.

title: Invariant discovery with counterexamples
connection: Search low-degree expressions constant under verified certificate transformations, rejecting candidates on fresh exact examples.
why: A discovered invariant can organize orbit structure and explain why some moves fail to connect families.
first_step: Solve linear equations for quadratic invariants of one transformation and check survivors symbolically.

title: Formal translation between word and fraction certificates
connection: Specify both sides of one short matrix-word equivalence and prove the conversion including sign and congruence conditions.
why: A checked bridge would allow discovery in one language and validation in another.
first_step: Select a length-two or length-three word and manually derive the forward and reverse formulas before formalizing.

title: Engel expansions as intermediate representations
connection: Compare multiplicative-denominator Engel expansions of 4/p with ordinary unit-fraction decompositions and possible regroupings.
why: Nested denominator structure may make some exact merges easier to describe.
first_step: Compute short Engel expansions for small primes and test adjacent-term merges into a single unit fraction.

title: Lüroth-style digit systems
connection: Check whether a rational expansion with consecutive-product denominators can be converted into a useful three-term ES ansatz.
why: The digit system offers a different exact decomposition grammar, not an automatic short representation.
first_step: Verify the precise Lüroth expansion formula and test finite rational examples for algebraically valid regroupings.

title: Ostrowski numeration of parameter choices
connection: Use continued-fraction-based numeration to encode auxiliary integers relative to p and a chosen modulus.
why: The digits may align with Euclidean recurrences and make congruence repair more local.
first_step: For one rational rotation, write several successful auxiliary values in Ostrowski coordinates and compare their digit patterns.

title: A precise question for an outside specialist
connection: Translate one ES subproblem into the native language of a finite-group, algorithmic-number-theory, or dynamics expert.
why: A sharply bounded lemma is more actionable than asking someone to solve the whole conjecture.
first_step: Draft a one-page question about bounded subset products hitting a specified residue, with a small worked ES example and no claim of equivalence beyond the derived map.

title: Polynomial continued fractions
connection: Compare short continued fractions over Fq[T] with the integer word formulations, retaining coefficient degree and unit information.
why: The Euclidean algorithm survives, but ordering and parity constraints change substantially.
first_step: Compute length-three expansions over F5[T] and identify which coefficient conditions correspond to the integer formulation.

title: Indefinite quadratic-form orbits
connection: Study indefinite quadratic slices using reduction and automorphisms rather than finite ellipsoid enumeration.
why: Infinite orbits may generate recurrent witnesses, with positivity handled along the orbit.
first_step: For one binary indefinite form arising from a slice, compute a fundamental automorphism and its residues modulo 8.

title: Thermodynamic formalism of the Gauss map restricted to length-3 continued fractions
connection: ES₅ ⟺ a certain rational has continued-fraction length λ ≤ 3. Thermodynamic formalism (Mayer transfer operator, Bowen's formula) controls the distribution of CF lengths over rationals with given denominator.
why: Hensley's theorem (Zaremba density) uses exactly this machinery; pointwise results for specific denominators are the analogue of what ES needs.
first_step: Read FRONTIER on ES₅ and write down exactly which rational r(p,·) must have λ ≤ 3; then check Hensley 'Continued fractions, Cantor sets, Hausdorff dimension' for any pointwise (not density) statement.

title: Frenkel–Kontorova / devil's staircase of the 'best C' function
connection: C_min(p) (smallest C with a winning divisor) as a function of p may show a staircase structure with plateaus at values tied to Mordell classes; devil's staircases arise from mode-locking in circle maps.
why: Mode-locking = rational rotation numbers = continued fractions, which is already an ES reformulation (ES₅).
first_step: Plot C_min(p) against p for p ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁷; look for plateau structure and its relation to p mod 840.

title: Word problem in SL₂(ℤ): ES as membership of a specific matrix in a product of three 'elementary' cosets
connection: Repo mentions SL₂ words. Membership-in-product-set problems in SL₂(ℤ) are decidable (automaticity of SL₂) and have automaton-theoretic structure; the 'length ≤ 3' condition of ES₅ is a bounded word length.
why: Automata for SL₂(ℤ) (via the free product ℤ/4 * ℤ/6) give a regular-language description of 'length ≤ 3 words'; the question becomes whether a regular language intersects a p-dependent set, which is sometimes handled by Büchi-type decidability over (ℕ, +, V_k).
first_step: Write the ES₅ word form as an explicit matrix product with entries depending on p; check whether the condition is 'matrix M_p is in L' for a regular L in the generator alphabet.

title: Error-correcting codes: solution sets as codewords, and ES as 'minimum distance ≥ 1 from the zero word'
connection: Define for each p the binary vector v_p ∈ {0,1}^K with v_p[C] = 1 if C wins. ES(p) for C ≤ K ⟺ v_p ≠ 0. The set {v_p} is a 'code'; its minimum weight (over p) and its dual structure may reveal linear constraints among the C's.
why: Linear constraints among win-events (over F₂) would be exactly the parity invariants that could force a win.
first_step: Compute v_p for K = 64 and p ≤ 10⁶; compute the F₂-rank of the matrix and look for low-weight dual codewords (parity checks).

title: Egyptian fraction 'Engel expansion' and 'Pierce expansion' of 4/p: alternative canonical expansions with ≤ 3 terms?
connection: Engel expansion writes x = 1/a₁ + 1/(a₁a₂) + 1/(a₁a₂a₃) + …; Pierce alternates signs. For 4/p, the Engel expansion's length and the possibility of truncation/modification to 3 unit fractions is an unexplored canonical form.
why: Canonical expansions with algebraic structure (Engel: a_{k+1} determined by a_k) might make 'length 3' a tractable condition like ES₅'s CF length.
first_step: Compute Engel expansions of 4/p for p ≤ 10⁴; count lengths; check whether a length-3 Engel expansion exists for all p (unlikely) or whether the Engel denominators relate to Type I/II parameters.

title: Stern–Brocot / Farey neighbours: 4/p's Farey parents and the two-term splitting 4/p = 1/x + (4x−p)/(px)
connection: Farey neighbours a/b, c/d with bc − ad = 1 give 1/(bd) = c/d − a/b; a unit-fraction-friendly structure. Writing 4/p as a sum of unit fractions via Farey-neighbour chains of length 3.
why: The repo has Farey items (bsA_farey_*); the free-lane twist: is there a 'Farey path' interpretation where ES = path of length 3 in the Farey graph from 4/p to 0 with unit-fraction steps? That's close to the CF/ES₅ form; worth making explicit.
first_step: git grep -il farey BRAINSTORM | head; then compute for p ≤ 1000 the Farey-graph distance from 4/p to 0 under 'subtract a unit fraction' moves.

title: Music/tilings: 4/p as a rhythm — Euclidean rhythms and unit-fraction tilings of the circle
connection: Tiling a circle of circumference 4 by three arcs of lengths p/x, p/y, p/z... i.e. 4 = p/x + p/y + p/z — a tiling of [0,4] by rational lengths with a common 'p' numerator. Euclidean rhythms (Toussaint) relate to Bjorklund's algorithm = Euclid's algorithm = continued fractions.
why: Recreational lens that lands on continued fractions again; perhaps a rhythmic 'evenness' measure corresponds to CF length ≤ 3.
first_step: Just note the reformulation; compute whether the Bjorklund rhythm E(4, p) decomposes into 3 'regular' sub-rhythms iff ES solution exists with specific structure — 15 minutes.
refs: Toussaint, 'The Euclidean algorithm generates traditional musical rhythms' (2005)

title: Analogy of analogy: ES ↔ Zaremba ↔ Markoff ↔ Apollonian — the 'thin orbit' quadrilateral; where does ES sit in the (orbit, expansion, obstruction) triangle?
connection: Zaremba (solved, claimed): thin semigroup orbit, expansion, no obstruction. Markoff mod p: group orbit, expansion, divisibility rigidity. Apollonian: thin group orbit, expansion, reciprocity obstruction (local-global FALSE). ES: no known group/semigroup, polylog count, reciprocity obstruction at squares. The missing ingredient is the orbit; the free-lane question: can ES certificates be realised as a thin *semigroup* orbit in SL₂(ℤ) or in a 2×2×2 cube structure, with p as a 'level'?
why: Pattern-matching across the four problems isolates exactly one missing ingredient (an orbit structure) — a concrete target for construction rather than proof.
first_step: Write the ES₅ CF form as a product of SL₂(ℤ) generators (Zaremba-style: p/q with partial quotients ≤ A ⟺ matrix in a semigroup orbit); identify what plays the role of 'q' and whether ES is 'λ ≤ 3' for a rational with *p-tied* numerator — then it's a *level* condition, not an orbit condition. Document the mismatch precisely.

title: Semigroup orbit reformulation: Type II certificates as products of two 'elementary' matrices in a congruence semigroup
connection: 4Cp + 1 = (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1). Consider matrices M_C(u) = [[4Cu − 1, ?],[?, ?]] in SL₂? E.g. the matrix [[4Cu−1, −u],[−4C·?..]] — find a representation where the product M_C(u)·M_C(v) has p as an entry. Try: A_u = [[1, u],[0, 1]]·[[1, 0],[−4C, 1]]·... Standard: the continued fraction [0; 4C, u, ...]? Let's just make it an experiment.
why: If Type II certificates are entries of products in a 2-generator semigroup (parametrised by C), then 'p appears as an entry' is a thin-orbit problem with the level 4C — same shape as Zaremba (where the semigroup is fixed and q is the entry). The novelty: the semigroup depends on C, but p must appear for SOME C — a union over C of thin orbits.
first_step: Find matrices in SL₂(ℤ) whose (1,1)-entry of a length-2 product is (4Cu−1)(4Cv−1) − 1)/(4C) = p for integers u,v (e.g. [[4Cu−1, u],[4C·?, ?]] with det 1 forces entries); if found, compare with the ES₅ word of length 3.

title: Bourgain–Kontorovich-style 'local-global for a thin semigroup orbit' in the C-direction: fix p, vary (u, v): p = 4Cuv − u − v
connection: Rewrite p = 4Cuv − u − v ⟹ for fixed C this is a quadratic form in (u, v) (indefinite: 4Cuv − u − v); p is represented by the 'form' Q_C(u,v) = 4Cuv − u − v for some C. Representation of p by one of a family of indefinite binary quadratic polynomials — a family of *quadratic* problems, each with a class-group structure (indefinite forms: Pell-type unit group acts on representations!).
why: For fixed C, representations of p by 4Cuv − u − v: complete the square: (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1) = 4Cp + 1; so it's the divisor problem again — but the INDEFINITE FORM viewpoint says: the 'automorphs' of the form act on solutions; the form 4Cuv − u − v has discriminant (4C)² — a *square* discriminant, so the form is degenerate (a product of linear forms) and its automorph group is trivial. OK so no Pell action — that's why no orbit. Document: 'the ES form has square discriminant; its automorph group is trivial; hence no Vieta/Pell dynamics'. This is a clean statement of the missing orbit.
first_step: Write it up as a lemma: every ES parametrisation (Type I, Type II, e-slice) has a quadratic form of square discriminant ⟹ no infinite automorphism group ⟹ no orbit dynamics. Check Type I: f·g = p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd — discriminant of the relevant form is −16c²d, NOT square — so Type I does have a class group (finite, ℚ(√−d)) but no infinite unit group. So the only rigid structure is the finite class group of ℚ(√−d), varying with d.

title: Numeration systems: Ostrowski numeration (based on the CF of a fixed irrational) and Zeckendorf — is there a numeration system in which 'n has an ES certificate' is a digit condition?
connection: Automatic-sequence-style question in a non-standard numeration: some sets defined by CF data (e.g. Beatty sequences) are recognisable in Ostrowski numeration (Hieronymi–Terry). ES₅ is a CF condition on a p-tied rational; maybe recognisable in a suitable numeration, making Walnut-style decision procedures applicable to sub-statements.
why: Long shot; but Ostrowski-automatic sets are a modern decidable class that includes CF-defined sets.
first_step: Read Hieronymi–Terry 'Ostrowski numeration systems, addition, and finite automata'; check if 'CF length of r(p) ≤ 3' can be phrased for p in a fixed Ostrowski system.
refs: Hieronymi–Terry, Notre Dame J. Formal Logic 2018

title: Collatz analogy: 'stopping time' of a certificate search as a function of p vs Collatz stopping times — both have log-ish expected values with no pointwise proof; what do Collatz researchers' heuristics (Tao's almost-all result via logarithmic density) suggest for ES?
connection: Tao (2019) proved almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values via a 'logarithmic density + invariant measure' argument; ES has almost-all results via sieve. The Collatz pointwise question remains open for the same 'no reservoir' reason. Structural comparison: Collatz has a dynamical system; ES has none (no orbit) — see the orbit-absence lemma. So ES is 'Collatz without the map'.
why: Comparison sharpens what ES lacks (a map) and what it has (algebra: factorisations); a hybrid (define a map on certificates) is the 'Lyapunov function' item.
first_step: Read Tao's Collatz paper intro for the heuristic model and see if the 'Syracuse random variable' method has an ES analogue (random model of the factorisation of 4Cp+1 as C varies — the Kubilius model item).
refs: Tao, 'Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values' (Forum Math Pi 2022)

title: Ellenberg–Venkatesh 'local-global for representations of quadratic forms by forms' as pointwise via ergodic theory
connection: EV proved local-global for representations of a quadratic form by another with an auxiliary splitting prime ↔ ES fibre as 'representation of p by a cubic form family'.
why: Precedent for pointwise results via unipotent dynamics; a Ratner-type input on an ES-associated homogeneous space would be new.
first_step: Check whether ES Type II slice (4uBC − u − B = p) is an orbit-counting problem on a homogeneous space SL₂(ℝ)×… (it is affine in C — maybe).

title: Hydrodynamic limit of certificate count as p → ∞ along residue classes
connection: Limit shape of the set of successful (log u/log p, log C/log p) ↔ the main-term density.
why: A limit shape theorem (empirical measure of certificates converges) for almost all p is plausibly provable and would describe where certificates live.
first_step: Plot the empirical measure of (log u, log C)/log p for successful pairs over many p; compare with 1/(uC) density prediction.

title: Ask Kontorovich/Stange/Rickards about thin-orbit local-global methods for polylog-count problems
connection: Apollonian/HKRS reciprocity obstructions ↔ T1 dictionary; they know which methods could handle sparse orbits.
why: Direct expert check on whether 'Question R' could ever drop to polylog regime.
first_step: Prepare a one-page summary of the T1 ↔ quadratic-reciprocity-obstruction parallel and ask for pointers.

title: Representation theory of SL₂(ℤ/4C): the Type II condition as a matrix coefficient
connection: SL₂ form [[a,p],[c,d]] with congruences ↔ the count is a matrix coefficient of the permutation representation on cosets.
why: Decomposing into irreducibles separates trivial (main term) and nontrivial (fluctuation) parts — the genus/BM split might be the 1-dim characters; higher irreps carry X(n).
first_step: For small c, compute the permutation representation and its character decomposition; identify which irreps carry the T1 cancellation.

title: Teichmüller / mapping class group dynamics: SL₂(ℤ) words as Dehn twists on a torus
connection: SL₂(ℤ) = mapping class group of the torus; ES₅ words as products of Dehn twists ↔ curves on a torus with intersection numbers tied to p.
why: Geometric reformulation: ES(p) ⟺ some simple closed curves with prescribed intersection numbers exist — curve-complex combinatorics might give existence arguments.
first_step: Translate an ES₅ word [[a,p],[c,d]] into a pair of simple closed curves on the torus with intersection number p; examine the constraint 'c ∈ 4ℕ, a ≡ d ≡ −1 mod c' geometrically.

title: Combinatorics on words: the Christoffel word / Sturmian structure of continued fraction certificates
connection: Christoffel words encode rationals a/b and their CF ↔ ES₅ CF length ≤ 3 words.
why: Word combinatorics (palindromes, standard factorisation of Christoffel words) may produce a combinatorial proof of existence of a short factorisation.
first_step: Compute Christoffel words of 4/p and of certificate rationals; look for standard factorisations corresponding to ES solutions.

title: ES words are generalised Frobenius numbers: tuv − u − v = g_t(u,v), the largest integer with ≤ t−1 representations by ⟨u,v⟩ (CHECKED)
connection: For coprime u,v the largest n with at most t−1 representations n = au + bv (a,b ≥ 0) is tuv − u − v (t = 1: Sylvester's uv − u − v) ↔ I3/ES₅ words p = tuv − u − v, and (★) is t = 4C: p = 4C·uB − u − B.
why: Puts ES (★)/I3 inside the Frobenius problem / numerical-semigroup theory: ES(★) ⟺ p is the 4C-th 'k-Frobenius number' of some 2-generated semigroup ⟨u,B⟩. That field has its own tools (Apéry sets, Popoviciu's formula, Ehrhart theory, denumerants) and literature on which integers occur as (k-)Frobenius numbers. Not found in repo by grep.
first_step: Verified for u,v < 12, t ≤ 4 (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check3.py). Next: search literature for 'k-Frobenius number' / 'generalized Frobenius number two generators' (Beck–Robins; Brown et al., J. Integer Seq. 2010 — check) and for 'which integers are Frobenius numbers'.

title: Apéry sets and the gap structure of ⟨u,B⟩: p as the maximal element of a 'level-(4C−1)' Apéry-type set
connection: Numerical semigroup S = ⟨u,B⟩: the set of n with exactly k representations has a known structure (shifted Apéry sets) ↔ p must be the top element of the k = 4C − 1 layer.
why: Semigroup-theoretic language may let one treat (u,B) as an unknown semigroup and p as a forced invariant — e.g. counting semigroups of given 'k-Frobenius number' (an inverse problem) could have a generating-function solution.
first_step: Compute, for n ≤ 10⁴, the number of pairs (u,B, t) with g_t(u,B) = n, t ≡ 0 mod 4, and compare with R(n); then look for a semigroup-enumeration generating function.

title: Counting numerical semigroups by Frobenius number (Backelin, Kaplan, Zhai) as a template for 'every p is a k-Frobenius number'
connection: The number of numerical semigroups with Frobenius number F grows like c·2^{F/2} (Backelin) ↔ here restricted to embedding dimension 2 (polylog many) with k-Frobenius.
why: The embedding-dimension-2 restriction collapses the count to divisor-type size (as expected); but allowing embedding dimension 3 semigroups (three generators) might correspond to richer ES-type certificates — check if a 3-generator k-Frobenius identity gives ES solutions.
first_step: Compute Frobenius numbers of 3-generated semigroups ⟨a,b,c⟩ in families and check whether some family's g(a,b,c) formula yields ES certificates (e.g. Type I parametrisation).

title: Type I as a Frobenius-type formula? Look for a semigroup interpretation of the Type I parametrisation
connection: Type II (★) is a 2-generator k-Frobenius identity ↔ Type I (f | p² + 4c²d …) may correspond to a different invariant (e.g. Frobenius number of ⟨a, b, c⟩ or genus of ⟨u,v⟩: genus = (u−1)(v−1)/2).
why: If Type I also has a semigroup meaning, ES would be 'p is one of a few semigroup invariants of some small semigroup' — a uniform language for all certificates.
first_step: Write the Type I solution family in ET variables and test whether p equals g_t, genus, or other standard invariants (e.g. number of gaps, conductor) of ⟨·,·⟩ with parameters from the solution.

title: Representation-count symmetry N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t on [0, g_t] (CHECKED): an involution attached to every ES word
connection: For coprime u,v and g_t = tuv − u − v, the denumerant satisfies N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t for all 0 ≤ n ≤ g_t (generalising symmetry of ⟨u,v⟩ at t = 1) ↔ every ES word p = g_t(u,v) carries the involution n ↦ p − n on representation data.
why: An explicit involution attached to each certificate is the raw material for windmill/parity arguments (G1 parity column); here the involution lives on representations of integers below p rather than on certificates — a different thick object (size ≍ p).
first_step: Verified for u,v ≤ 8, t ≤ 4 (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check3.py). Next: look for a global involution on pairs (n, representation) over all (u,v) whose fixed points correspond to certificates of p; test fixed-point parity on p < 10³.

title: ES words are exactly Frobenius numbers of glued semigroups ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩
connection: Johnson/Brauer–Shockley gluing gives g(⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩) = t·g(u,v) + (t−1)(u+v) = tuv − u − v when gcd(u,v) = gcd(t,u+v) = 1 (checked by brute force on 488 triples, scripts/z52b_signature_frob_check.py). So the (★) line (words p = 4C·u·B − u − B, which implies ES but itself fails at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰) ⟺ p is the Frobenius number of a 3-generated numerical semigroup ⟨4Cu, 4CB, u+B⟩; for (★) words gcd(4C, u+B) = gcd(4C, p) = 1 automatically. The other ES word slices (coordinate in 8ℤ − p, or the 4ℤ coordinate not in the t slot) need a different semigroup family.
why: Rosales–García-Sánchez–García-García–Jiménez Madrid proved every positive integer is the Frobenius number of SOME 3-generated semigroup: the (★) slice of ES is a restriction of a solved universality theorem to a structured sub-family (complete intersections glued from a 2-generated piece); finding semigroup families for the other ES slices would give a full semigroup reformulation of ES.
first_step: Read Rosales et al. (Math. Scand. 94 (2004) 5–12): which 3-generator family does their construction use for odd g, and can it be forced into the shape ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ with 4 | t?
refs: J. C. Rosales, P. A. García-Sánchez, J. I. García-García, J. M. Jiménez Madrid, Every positive integer is the Frobenius number of a numerical semigroup with three generators, Math. Scand. 94 (2004) 5–12 (https://journals.msp.org/mscand/article/view/792)

title: Symmetric 3-generated semigroups = complete intersections (Herzog): ES as a symmetric-Frobenius representation problem
connection: Herzog: 3-generated symmetric numerical semigroups are complete intersections, i.e. gluings ⟨d·a, d·b, c⟩ with c ∈ ⟨a,b⟩, gcd(d,c) = 1, whose Frobenius numbers are d(ab − a − b) + (d − 1)c. ES words are the slice c = a + b; other c = αa + βb give other trilinear words dab − a(d − (d−1)α) − b(d − (d−1)β).
why: Gives a natural ambient family (all symmetric 3-generated Frobenius numbers = all odd numbers?) containing the ES words; the question 'which (α,β) slices are universal on primes' is a clean ladder of problems, some maybe solved.
first_step: Enumerate, for odd n ≤ 10⁶, which (α,β) ∈ {0,1,2}² slices of d(ab−a−b)+(d−1)(αa+βb) with 4 | d represent n; compare failure sets with U(n)/T1.
refs: unverified: Herzog 1970, Generators and relations of abelian semigroups and semigroup rings (manuscripta math.)

title: Rødseth/Greenberg 3-generator Frobenius algorithm vs. ES₅ continued-fraction length
connection: The Rødseth algorithm computes g(a,b,c) via a negative-continued-fraction (Euclid) expansion of a ratio mod a; for ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ that expansion is short. Compare with λ(p) ≤ 3 (F17).
why: If the Rødseth expansion of the glued semigroup is exactly the length-3 negative CF of the ES₅ form, the semigroup literature (Kannan, Ramírez Alfonsín) becomes a dictionary for ES₅.
first_step: Run Rødseth's algorithm symbolically on ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ and record the CF; check against the BOARD2_SLATE ES₅ slice definitions.
refs: unverified: Rødseth 1978, On a linear diophantine problem of Frobenius (J. reine angew. Math.)

title: Genus/Sylvester count of the ES semigroup as a second invariant attached to each witness
connection: Each ES witness (t,u,v) gives a symmetric semigroup S with genus (gaps) (g+1)/2 = (p+1)/2 and an Apéry set of size min generator; these invariants are fixed by p, so ES asks for a semigroup with prescribed Frobenius number and prescribed shape.
why: Counting numerical semigroups by genus is a mature field (Kaplan, Zhai's Fibonacci-like growth); ES asks for one member of a structured subclass among ~φ^g semigroups of genus g — a sparse-subfamily existence question.
first_step: Check OEIS/semigroup tables (e.g. GAP package numericalsgps) for counts of complete-intersection semigroups with given Frobenius number.
refs: unverified: Zhai 2013, Fibonacci-like growth of numerical semigroups of a given genus (Semigroup Forum)

title: IMO 2007/5 Vieta jumping (4ab−1 | (4a²−1)² ⇒ a = b) as an involution proof of T1-type statements
connection: The IMO problem is the same form 4ab − 1 as level-4 ES divisors (d ≡ −1 mod 4). Its standard solution is Vieta jumping (infinite descent on an involution orbit).
why: Vieta-jumping proofs give a dynamical (descent) proof of non-existence; reversing the descent (ascent) is a way to generate witnesses — F38. Note the ES word itself is multilinear (degree 1 in each variable), so the Vieta involution lives on an auxiliary quadratic, as in the IMO solution.
first_step: Identify the auxiliary quadratic in the IMO solution ((4a²−1)² = k(4ab−1), quadratic in a) whose Vieta involution proves the level-4 statement, and write its analogue for level 4C divisors d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cm²+1.

title: Descartes/Soddy: three mutually tangent circles of radii x,y,z have inner Soddy curvature 1/x+1/y+1/z + 2√((x+y+z)/xyz)
connection: ES fixes the linear part to 4/n; rationality of the Soddy curvature additionally needs (x+y+z)/(xyz) to be a rational square. Links ES to Apollonian-type curvature questions (F08 via HKRS).
why: A sub-family of ES solutions inside integral Apollonian configurations would inherit thin-orbit tools.
first_step: Count ES solutions (p ≤ 10⁵) where (x+y+z)·xyz is a square; if non-empty, look for Apollonian structure.

title: Shrinking-target / hitting-time for the Gauss map: λ(p) ≤ 3 as 'some orbit hits a target in ≤ 3 steps'
connection: ES₅: for each p there is q with p/q of continued-fraction length ≤ 3 (with constraints). In dynamics language: some rational point of denominator p reaches a target set within 3 Gauss-map steps.
why: Effective equidistribution of rationals with denominator p under the Gauss map (Ustinov, Bykovskii) could give counts of such q with a main term ≍ log²p.
first_step: Check Ustinov's results on the statistics of continued-fraction lengths of a/p for fixed p (number of a with length ≤ k).
refs: unverified: Ustinov, On the statistical properties of elements of continued fractions (Doklady)

title: Collatz (Tao 2019): almost all orbits attain almost bounded values via logarithmic density — the exceptional-set-improvement analogue
connection: ∀n conjecture (F01), almost-all known (F05), huge verification (F23), heuristic support (F24). Tao's key was changing the measure (logarithmic density) to gain an approximate invariance.
why: ES's exceptional set bound is stuck at exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) (F40); a change of averaging measure (logarithmic weights in p, or weighting by the BM main term) might likewise gain invariance.
first_step: Recompute the ES exceptional-set argument with logarithmic density in n and see whether the 3/4 barrier changes.

title: ES as a Hurwitz-type equation with a Vieta group: orbit counts per n
connection: Hurwitz equations Σx_i² = a·Πx_i have finitely many fundamental solutions per (n,a) generating trees under Vieta moves; ES's word set has a forest structure (F39). Counting fundamental solutions vs. n is a solved problem type. Caveat: tuv − u − v and the ES cubic are multilinear, so classical Vieta root swaps do not exist on them; the analogue must use other involutions/birational moves.
why: If ES words admit a finite 'fundamental domain' per p, existence reduces to existence of a fundamental solution with bounded size.
first_step: Search for involutions or birational moves on (t,u,v) preserving tuv − u − v = p (e.g. moves through the divisor pairing d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d, swaps across levels) and compute orbit structure for p ≤ 10⁴.
refs: unverified: Hurwitz 1907, Über eine Aufgabe der unbestimmten Analysis

title: Ordering continuants by local transformations
connection: The operation increasing continuants in arXiv:1608.08322 matches ES F16/F17/F32: bounded continued-fraction words encode integers, and local word changes control their size.
why: A controlled transformation on the ES length-three word may normalize coordinates or push a witness into a useful congruence class.
first_step: Read the operation in the paper and test whether an analogous adjacent-letter move preserves n=tuv−u−v while changing the coordinate residue.

title: Periodic continuant formulas and ES residue periodicity
connection: The explicit periodic-continuant formulas in arXiv:2001.06213 match ES F16/F17/F03, since periodic continued-fraction words can encode structured congruence families.
why: This is a concrete identity toolkit for testing whether periodic ES word patterns generate infinite residue-class families.
first_step: Use the paper's periodic formula on a short periodic word and compare its resulting n-values modulo the ES covering modulus 840.

title: Continued-fraction convergence bounds for word certificates
connection: The continuant estimates in arXiv:2106.03789 concern extremal sizes of structured continued fractions, matching ES F17/F32 and the small-witness feature F04's sparse-count setting.
why: Size bounds can test whether a word construction has polynomial-size denominators, a prerequisite for a useful ES certificate family.
first_step: Read the extremal bound and apply it to length-three ES words with the required coordinate congruences; record the resulting denominator exponent.

title: Integral orbit tree versus finite ES residue covers
connection: The Markoff–Hurwitz positive-solution asymptotics in arXiv:2605.05075 match ES F13/F38/F34: an infinite orbit tree is a contrast to ES's need to cover every prime by families.
why: It suggests measuring whether a finite set of ES moves produces enough residue classes or only a thin orbit.
first_step: Compute the mod-840 action of candidate ES coordinate involutions and compare the orbit's residue coverage with the known Mordell covering.

title: Stern continuants and orbit-growth bounds
connection: The explicit transformation/order methods for continuants in arXiv:1608.08322 match ES F16/F17/F38 and the tree-like certificate organization F39.
why: If ES word transformations form a graph, extremal continuant growth could bound the size and depth of its search tree.
first_step: Build the graph of length-three ES word moves induced by continued-fraction identities and test whether the extremal operation from the paper bounds depth at fixed n.

title: A matrix-orbit test for ES certificate connectivity
connection: Markoff matrix/tree encodings in arXiv:0709.1499 match ES F18/F38/F39 and F32: the central question can be reframed as whether short transformations connect all required certificate states.
why: This suggests a finite-state or orbit-connectivity experiment on congruence reductions, directly aligned with the ES word-graph viewpoint.
first_step: Define vertices as ES word certificates modulo a small modulus and test whether candidate matrix generators connect every admissible residue state.

title: Bounded continued-fraction words and thin ES families
connection: The extremal continuant results in arXiv:2106.03789 match ES F17/F30/F32: restricted words generate thin infinite families with controlled growth, analogous to known ES families that do not yet cover all primes.
why: It offers estimates for the cost and density of one certificate family without treating thinness as a reason to discard it.
