first_step: Apply the paper's extremal bounds to an ES word family such as periodic partial quotients and estimate the number of primes it could cover up to X.

title: Zaremba: thin semigroup growth versus universal coverage
connection: Zaremba shares F01, F17, F22, F30: universal denominator coverage is conjectured, while restricted-CF semigroups first yield large/thin sets. ES similarly has thin proved prime families but no all-prime rung (F30).
why: Growth and expansion estimates for a structured thin set may suggest how to move from infinitely many ES prime families toward density or coverage.
first_step: Extract the precise denominator-count lower bound in the cited paper and ask whether a corresponding count of ES primes covered by bounded parameter boxes is accessible.

title: Zaremba feature flip: bounded partial quotients
connection: Zaremba matches ES’s universal-existence goal, matrix/continued-fraction structure, and computational checks (F01,F18,F23), but demands bounded partial quotients (F17w) rather than ES’s bounded CF length. This feature-flip isolates a stronger regularity condition.
why: Understanding what bounded digits buy—expansion and uniformity—could identify which ES CF constraints are essential versus convenient.
first_step: Compare the matrix products in Zaremba’s proof with ES₅ matrices and record exactly where a uniform digit bound enters.

title: Collatz parity vectors as finite-word certificates
connection: The Collatz problem shares F16w, F22, F32, F23: finite parity words encode trajectories and permit certificate-style computation for a universal integer claim. ES has fixed polynomial/word forms and short certificates (F16,F32).
why: The disciplined separation of word constraints, congruences, and positivity may inspire an ES certificate search with independently checkable proof objects.
first_step: Write a tiny enumerator for ES n=tuv−u−v certificates by bounded word/parameter height and compare its pruning by congruences with Collatz parity-vector pruning.

title: Markov triples: mutation trees and orbit enumeration
connection: Markov triples share ES’s integral cubic equation, involutive transformations, thin witness families, and finite checks (F13,F30,F38,F23). Mutation organizes infinitely many solutions from a small seed.
why: A mutation-orbit perspective could reveal whether ES solutions partition into manageable parameter orbits rather than isolated divisor certificates.
first_step: Enumerate low-height ES triples modulo permutation and test for simple rational transformations preserving the defining cubic after fixing n.

title: Three-generator Frobenius numbers as sparse witnesses
connection: The 3-generator Frobenius problem shares F01,F10,F23,F32: arithmetic objects are characterized by integer parameters and modular/divisibility constraints, with finite certificates and computational catalogs. ES similarly searches thin divisor witnesses for each prime.
why: Apéry-set methods convert semigroup membership into finite residue-class data, potentially useful for organizing ES divisors by residue.
first_step: Read a three-generator Frobenius formula and test an Apéry-style residue table for ES’s tied divisor integer 4Cp+1.

title: Numerical semigroup Apéry sets and finite residue certificates
connection: The Frobenius problem shares F03,F10,F32: congruence classes modulo a generator reduce an infinite additive semigroup question to finite residue representatives. ES witness divisibility similarly reduces to residue classes and a finite certificate.
why: Apéry-set bookkeeping is a concrete way to ensure residue coverage is complete rather than heuristic.
first_step: For small primes, tabulate ES’s admissible divisors by residue class modulo 4C and compare the completeness proof format with Apéry-set closure.

title: SL₂(Z) semigroup membership as bounded-word reachability
connection: Matrix-semigroup membership shares F16w,F18,F32,F23: existence asks for a finite word producing a target matrix, with short certificates and decidable bounded searches. ES has a prescribed-entry SL₂ formulation and bounded certificate length.
why: Automata/word-search tools can enumerate structured ES matrix products and exploit congruence states before large integers arise.
first_step: Encode the ES matrix identity as generators and run breadth-first search modulo small moduli, retaining only states compatible with the target entry.

title: Lüroth expansions and finite digit alphabets
connection: Lüroth and continued-fraction expansions share F17,F18,F32: digits encode rational values by short arithmetic words, with bounded-digit variants producing thin sets. ES also has bounded-length CF/SL₂ descriptions.
why: Alternative expansion algorithms may give a more natural parametrization of positive rational decompositions than continued fractions.
first_step: Search for a Lüroth representation of 4/p with constrained first digits and test whether three digit choices imply an ES decomposition.

title: Zaremba: transfer-operator counting for restricted digits
connection: Restricted-CF denominator problems share F17,F18,F22,F24: thin matrix semigroups are counted via digit words and growth heuristics. ES’s bounded CF length and matrix-entry target invite analogous transfer operators.
why: A transfer operator may estimate how many ES-compatible words exist at a given prime, rather than merely count all integer triples.
first_step: Define a transfer operator for ES’s allowed three-step matrix digits and calculate its predicted count against small-prime data.

title: Collatz: density notions and logarithmic sampling
connection: Collatz and ES share F05,F21,F23,F24: strong almost-all/computational evidence leaves pointwise exceptional inputs unresolved. Tao’s logarithmic-density approach makes the quantifier gap explicit.
why: Comparing natural and logarithmic density may tell whether ES exceptional primes are genuinely sparse in the metric relevant to divisor-counting estimates.
first_step: Compute the logarithmic count of ES primes lacking each fixed certificate family over existing bounded data and compare with natural-density counts.

title: Kourovka group problems: SL₂(Z) word reachability
connection: Group word problems share F16w,F18,F32: whether a target element is represented by a word has a short explicit certificate and congruence quotients provide cheap tests. ES has a prescribed-entry SL₂ reachability form.
why: Quotient-group obstructions and normal forms can identify necessary conditions or canonical representatives for ES matrix words.
first_step: Take the ES generator matrices, compute their images in SL₂(Z/mZ) for small m, and compare reachable target-entry states by prime residue.

title: Zaremba and ES: finite alphabet versus finite word length
connection: Both Zaremba and ES use continued fractions and SL₂ words (F17,F18,F32), but Zaremba constrains the digit alphabet while ES constrains word length and matrix entries. This feature flip isolates alphabet complexity from length complexity.
why: Comparing the two constraints may show whether ES can be attacked using a finite alphabet despite variable intermediate parameters.
first_step: Compute partial quotients of the ES₅ representations for small primes and test for a finite digit alphabet covering a positive fraction.

title: Continued fractions and bounded-length Diophantine representations
connection: Bounded continued-fraction problems share F16, F17, F32 and encode integers through short recurrences.
why: Short-CF classification may produce new finite families of ES certificates or expose the exact exceptional parameter set.
first_step: Translate the ES₅ formulation into continuants and search for a theorem bounding the omitted length-three cases.

title: Golsefidy–Varjú superstrong approximation for the ES₅ semigroup
connection: Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú prove expansion for perfect groups' congruence quotients; ES₅ words generate a semigroup in SL₂(ℤ) whose Zariski closure and congruence images are computable.
why: Determines whether the ES₅ semigroup has full congruence image mod every q (local-global input).
first_step: Compute the Zariski closure and mod-q images of the semigroup generated by the ES₅ letters for small q.
refs: Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú, Expansion in perfect groups, GAFA 22 (2012)

title: Magee–Oh–Winter uniform congruence counting for Schottky semigroups
connection: MOW give uniform spectral gap/congruence counting for thin Schottky semigroups; underlying tool for Zaremba-type local-global.
why: If ES₅ admits a Schottky-semigroup formulation with unbounded alphabet truncated at height T, uniform counting mod q gives local-global for almost all.
first_step: Check whether truncating ES₅ letters to digits ≤ A yields a Schottky semigroup and compute its Hausdorff dimension δ_A as A grows.
refs: Magee–Oh–Winter, Uniform congruence counting for Schottky semigroups in SL2(Z), Crelle 753 (2019)

title: Bourgain–Fuchs / Bourgain–Kontorovich density-one Apollonian method for ES siblings
connection: Positive-density and density-one results for Apollonian curvatures use thin-orbit circle methods with a quadratic subfamily (shifted binary forms); ES certificates are also quadratic-form values (p² + 4c²d).
why: Transfer of the 'quadratic subfamily + large sieve' trick to ES certificate families.
first_step: Identify a sub-family of ES certificates that is a shifted binary quadratic form in two free parameters at fixed p, and apply the BK almost-all argument.
refs: Bourgain–Kontorovich, On the local-global conjecture for integral Apollonian gaskets, Invent. Math. 196 (2014)

title: Lindenstrauss–Mohammadi–Wang polynomially effective unipotent equidistribution
connection: LMW (2022) give polynomially effective equidistribution for one-parameter unipotent orbits in SL₂(ℝ)×SL₂(ℝ)/Γ and SL₂(ℂ)/Γ-type spaces; ES Type II solutions are SL₂(ℤ) matrices [[f,a],[b,f′]] with ab = 4c²dp and f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd), i.e. lattice points in a thin region of SL₂.
why: Effective rates are the prerequisite for counting lattice points in shrinking/thin regions (polylog many expected).
first_step: Write the Type II count as a count of Γ₀(4cd)-points in a region of SL₂(ℝ) depending on p and estimate its volume vs LMW error terms.
refs: Lindenstrauss–Mohammadi–Wang, Effective equidistribution for some one parameter unipotent flows, arXiv:2211.11099

title: Einsiedler–Margulis–(Mohammadi–)Venkatesh effective equidistribution of closed semisimple orbits
connection: EMV/EMMV give effective equidistribution of closed orbits of semisimple groups (e.g. SO(Q) for ternary Q) with polynomial rates; ES has ternary-form and quaternion reformulations.
why: Closed-orbit equidistribution yields local-global for representations of large integers by forms — with effective rates, potentially of a whole genus.
first_step: Pick the repo's ternary/quaternion ES reformulation (QUATERNION_ES.md) and identify the closed orbit whose equidistribution would give the needed representations.
refs: Einsiedler–Margulis–Venkatesh, Effective equidistribution for closed orbits of semisimple groups on homogeneous spaces, Invent. Math. 177 (2009), arXiv:0708.4040
Einsiedler–Margulis–Mohammadi–Venkatesh, Effective equidistribution and property (τ), JAMS 33 (2020), arXiv:1503.05884

title: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth cycle integrals for ES₅ geodesic data
connection: DIT express traces of modular functions over closed geodesics (indefinite forms) as coefficients of mock modular forms; ES₅/CF-length data is geodesic (Hirzebruch–Jung, Dedekind) data of rationals tied to p.
why: A mock-modular generating function for CF-statistics could encode ES₅ counts with exact modular transformation laws.
first_step: Compute the DIT-style generating function Σ_D Tr_D(f) for f = indicator-like modular function and check whether CF length-3 counts appear.
refs: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, Cycle integrals of the j-function and mock modular forms, Ann. Math. 173 (2011)

title: Ramanujan Machine-style search for polynomial-CF identities producing ES₅ words
connection: The Ramanujan Machine (Raayoni et al., Nature 2021) searches polynomial continued fractions for constant identities; ES₅ solutions are short CF words with entries polynomial in parameters (Mordell families).
why: Automated search over polynomial CF word families could find new parametric families covering more residue classes.
first_step: Enumerate length-3 ES₅ words whose entries are degree-≤2 polynomials in t with small coefficients and record which residue classes mod 840·k they cover.
refs: Raayoni et al., Generating conjectures on fundamental constants with the Ramanujan Machine, Nature 590 (2021)

title: OAI 018 Margulis–Platonov (claimed) — normal subgroups of SL₂ over global fields for ES words
connection: OAI 018 claims Margulis–Platonov over number fields; normal-subgroup structure of arithmetic groups matters for congruence-subgroup and thin-group questions about ES₅ words.
why: Very indirect; listed for completeness of the SL₂-word line.
first_step: Close unless an ES SL₂ formulation needs non-congruence normal subgroups.

title: Word-map surjectivity (Larsen–Shalev; Ore conjecture) for ES₅ word shapes
connection: Larsen–Shalev show word maps w: G^k → G are surjective (or nearly) for large finite simple groups; ES₅ is a specific word shape with constrained letters in SL₂.
why: Surjectivity of the ES word map on SL₂(𝔽_q) (with letter constraints) is the local-at-q statement; failures at small q explain local obstructions.
first_step: Define the constrained ES₅ word map over 𝔽_q and compute its image size for q ≤ 100.
refs: Larsen–Shalev, Word maps and Waring type problems, JAMS 22 (2009)

title: Helfgott growth in SL₂(𝔽_p) for the set of ES₅ letters
connection: Helfgott: generating sets A of SL₂(𝔽_p) satisfy |AAA| ≥ |A|^{1+δ} unless A is nearly the group; the ES₅ letter set at p is a specific subset.
why: Growth explains how quickly length-k words cover the group; ES fixes k = 3 so the growth exponent needed is computable.
first_step: Measure |A|, |A²|, |A³| mod small primes for the ES₅ letter set restricted to letters of height ≤ p.
refs: Helfgott, Growth and generation in SL2(Z/pZ), Ann. Math. 167 (2008)

title: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh effective ×a×b for multiplicative semigroups mod q
connection: BLMV give effective equidistribution of orbits of the multiplicative semigroup ⟨a,b⟩ acting on ℤ/q (Furstenberg ×2×3 discrete analogue); ES e-slices ask whether −1 lies in a product set built from a few multiplicative generators mod e.
why: Shows when a 2-generator multiplicative semigroup fills (ℤ/q)^× — the 'enough generators' threshold relevant to pooling slices.
first_step: Compute, for e-slices at hard primes, the size of the semigroup generated by the two smallest prime factors of N mod e.
refs: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh, Some effective results for ×a×b, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 29 (2009)

title: Tao's Collatz 'almost bounded orbits' technique for greedy-with-choice Egyptian algorithms
connection: Tao (2019) analysed a 3-adic Syracuse random variable to show almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values; ES solutions are produced by greedy-type algorithms (choose x ≈ n/4, recurse on the remainder) whose residue dynamics resemble Syracuse.
why: A stabilisation argument for the remainder's residue distribution could show 'greedy with bounded look-ahead succeeds for almost all n in log density' — and identify the structure of failures.
first_step: Implement the greedy-with-choice algorithm (x = ⌈n/4⌉ + k, k ≤ K) and record the residue distribution of remainders at each step for p ≤ 10^7.
refs: Tao, Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values, Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022), arXiv:1909.03562

title: Host–Kra / Frantzikinakis ergodic structure for multiplicative ES colourings
connection: Host–Kra factors describe multiple ergodic averages; Frantzikinakis–Host apply them to multiplicative functions; the colouring of n by 'ES shape type' is multiplicatively closed (solutions lift to multiples).
why: A Furstenberg-correspondence model of the ES shape colouring could show forced configurations in each colour class.
first_step: Define the colouring n ↦ (minimal certificate type) and test partition-regularity-type configurations numerically.
refs: Host–Kra, Nonconventional ergodic averages and nilmanifolds, Ann. Math. 161 (2005)

title: Spanning-tree values and Zaremba (Chan–Kontorovich–Pak) applied to fan graphs
connection: Chan–Kontorovich–Pak prove exponential growth of the set of spanning-tree counts of n-vertex planar graphs via continued fractions, thin orbits and Zaremba. ES₅ asks the same kind of question for continuants of length 3 with a sign condition.
why: It is the nearest proved theorem in which spanning-tree counts and continued fractions are linked through thin-orbit methods. Their graphs realise numerators of CFs, as our fan does for HJ length 3.
first_step: Read arXiv:2411.18782 §2 (graph ↔ CF dictionary). Check whether their construction realises a prescribed numerator p with a prescribed denominator class (A/p) = −1 at bounded length.
refs: arXiv:2411.18782 (Chan–Kontorovich–Pak, Spanning trees and continued fractions)

title: Casson–Walker invariant / Dedekind sum of L(p,A) restricted to HJ-length-3 A
connection: λ_CW(L(p,q)) is a Dedekind sum s(q,p) up to normalisation, and Rademacher-type congruences tie 12p·s(q,p) mod 8 to (q/p). On words, s(A,p) has a closed form in (t,u,v) by Dedekind reciprocity.
why: It gives an explicit integer-valued topological invariant of the word whose residue mod 8 is the ES sign. Sums over words then become sums of a topological invariant.
first_step: Derive s(tu−1, p) in closed form from three applications of reciprocity; compare with DEDEKIND_ES §4.

title: Cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A) with a 3-curve resolution and non-residue A
connection: p/A = [[v,t,u]] is the minimal resolution chain (−v,−t,−u) of the cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A). ES₅(p) ⇔ some 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has exactly 3 exceptional curves.
why: Singularity theory controls resolution lengths via Riemenschneider duality, P-resolutions and smoothing components (KSB). The ES sign is a Galois-type datum: is 1/p(1,A) isomorphic over a quadratic twist to 1/p(1,1)?
first_step: Compute embedding dimension and Riemenschneider dual lengths for A ∈ L₃(p); test whether the dual-chain length distribution differs between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Frobenius-class form: uv | n+u+v ⇔ n is in the 'Frobenius shadow' of the numerical semigroup ⟨u,v⟩
connection: n = tuv−u−v ⇔ n ≡ −(u+v) (mod uv). If gcd(u,v) = 1 (automatic for interior words at a prime n), Popoviciu's formula gives exactly t−1 representations of n as au+bv (a,b ≥ 0), and uv−u−v is the Frobenius number. Without coprimality this fails (t = u = v = 2, n = 4). ES₅ words are pairs (u,v) whose denumerant at n is in the Frobenius residue class, plus a sign condition.
why: The theory of numerical semigroups and denumerants (Popoviciu, Sylvester, Ramírez Alfonsín) gives a new vocabulary for the forest F_p (uv | p+u+v), with generating-function tools.
first_step: Express the ES₅ sign in terms of (u,v,n) via denumerant data; check whether Σ_{(u,v)} sign·q^n has a Popoviciu-type generating function (∏ 1/(1−q^u)(1−q^v) restricted to a class).
refs: Ramírez Alfonsín, The Diophantine Frobenius Problem (2005)

title: Christoffel/Sturmian word of slope A/p with three runs
connection: HJ length r(p/A) is a run-length statistic of the Christoffel word of slope A/p (equivalently the cutting sequence of the segment to (p,A)). ES₅ asks for a non-residue A whose Christoffel word has the minimal 3-block structure.
why: Combinatorics on words has exact results on Christoffel words, palindromes and standard factorizations, which might give explicit constructions of A with prescribed structure, for instance via palindromic closure.
first_step: Express r(p/A) = 3 as a factorisation condition on the Christoffel word; test whether the Lothaire standard factorisation relates the two halves to (A/p).
refs: Lothaire, Algebraic Combinatorics on Words, ch. 2

title: Plumbing calculus moves (blow-up/blow-down of ±1 curves) as certificate transport
connection: Kirby calculus moves change a plumbing chain without changing the boundary lens space. The boundary words (letters = 1) of LENGTH_THREE are formal words that become interior after blow-downs.
why: This gives a topological interpretation of the repo's boundary/interior word distinction and of 'transport' moves between certificates (boundary-preserving blow-ups do not change |det|, so transport between different n needs a non-boundary-preserving move such as a surgery/cobordism step; identify which).
first_step: Map LENGTH_THREE formal words (letter 1) to blow-down sequences; check whether ES transport laws (TRANSPORT_LAW.md) are Kirby moves.

title: Farey-graph geodesic of length 3 in the non-residue class
connection: HJ length r(p/A) is (up to normalisation) a combinatorial distance-type statistic in the Farey graph from ∞ to p/A via a specific path type. ES₅ asks whether the Farey ball of 'HJ radius 3' around ∞ contains a vertex p/A with A a QNR.
why: The Farey graph is hyperbolic geometry's combinatorial skeleton, and its metric theory (Beardon–Hockman–Short) is well developed.
first_step: Compare r(p/A) with Farey distance d(∞, p/A) for p < 10⁴; check whether the ES₅ condition is a Farey-distance condition for a known metric.

title: Lyness 5-cycle with a coefficient: integrable map whose integer orbits are ES₅ words
connection: The pentagon Ptolemy relations with one frozen side N give a period-5 birational map (a Lyness-type recurrence x_{k+1}x_{k−1} = x_k + c_k with c ∈ {1,N}). Integer orbits are words. Lyness maps have an invariant cubic (elliptic) fibration.
why: Discrete integrable systems give invariants and elliptic fibrations of such maps; the invariant of the coefficient-N Lyness cycle gives each word a 'conserved energy', possibly with arithmetic meaning.
first_step: Compute the invariant rational function of the (1,1,1,1,N) Lyness cycle (sympy). Evaluate it on words and look for a link with the sign or with t.

title: Vallée's dynamical analysis of Euclidean algorithms (by-excess algorithm) with a quadratic character
connection: The HJ expansion is the 'by-excess' Euclidean algorithm. Vallée's transfer-operator method gives limit laws for costs such as length. ES₅ asks for the extreme value: min length over A in the non-residue class equals 3.
why: It is the native analysis-of-algorithms framework; twisting transfer operators by Dirichlet characters is done in Baladi–Vallée-type works.
first_step: Look up whether the by-excess algorithm's length distribution has been studied with a character twist (Baladi–Vallée 2005 for Gauss map; Dolgopyat estimates).

title: Backward-CF (Rényi-type) map T(x) = ⌈1/x⌉ − 1/x: infinite invariant measure and orbit length 3
connection: The HJ expansion is generated by a backward-CF (Rényi-type) map with an infinite invariant measure (parabolic fixed point). The coordinate convention matters: in the variable x = A/p the map T(x) = ⌈1/x⌉ − 1/x reproduces the HJ step, whereas the map x ↦ 1/(1−x) − ⌊⋯⌋ started at A/p does not (5/17 takes 4 steps, but its HJ length is 3). Short orbits to 0 in 3 steps are the ES₅ words.
why: Infinite-ergodic-theory tools (Aaronson, Thaler) describe return statistics near the parabolic point, and ES words are 'fast escapes', the complementary regime.
first_step: Compute the measure of points with exactly 3-step Rényi orbits to the cusp at resolution 1/p; compare with |L₃(p)|/p.
refs: Aaronson, An Introduction to Infinite Ergodic Theory (1997)

title: Mayer/Gauss–Kuzmin–Wirsing transfer operator twisted by (·/p): spectral gap for character sums over CF sets
connection: Character sums over sets defined by CF conditions can be studied by transfer operators with a character twist (as in Bourgain–Kontorovich and Dolgopyat). A spectral gap gives cancellation in Σ_{A: CF condition} χ(A).
why: It is the native way to get cancellation for CF-defined sets, but works for growing lengths, not length 3. Recorded as the nearest tool.
first_step: Record the length threshold L(p) beyond which twisted transfer-operator methods give non-trivial Σ_{A ∈ S_L(p)} (A/p); compare with λ(p) data.
refs: Mayer 1991 (transfer operator of the Gauss map)

title: Hilbert modular / Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles for the pair (A, A*) with AA* = tp+1
connection: Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles T_N on Hilbert modular surfaces have intersection numbers given by class numbers. Pairs (A,A*) with AA* = tp + 1 are points of a 'norm' condition that might be intersection points of T_N with a modular curve.
why: Hirzebruch–Zagier gives exact intersection numbers as coefficients of modular forms; if certificates are intersection points, their count is a known modular coefficient.
first_step: Check whether pairs (A, A*) with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t) and AA* = tp+1 are naturally CM points / intersection points on X(1) × X(1) (i.e. on a Hecke correspondence T_{tp+1}).
refs: Hirzebruch–Zagier, Intersection numbers of curves on Hilbert modular surfaces (Invent. 1976)

title: Hecke correspondence T_{tp+1} on X(1) × X(1) and ES words as its points with level structure
connection: Pairs of lattices with cyclic isogeny of degree N_t = tp+1 form the modular curve X₀(N_t). A word is a factorisation N_t = A·A* with congruences mod t, which is a Γ₀/Γ₁-level datum.
why: It gives ES₅ a moduli interpretation: level-t structures on isogenies of degree tp + 1. Moduli-theoretic counts (Riemann–Hurwitz on X₀) are exact.
first_step: Write the bijection {words of level t} ↔ {points on a specified cover of X₀(N_t) over ℤ}; check whether the sign is a Galois/Atkin–Lehner action.

title: Quadratic residue codes: ES₅ failure as S₃(p) ⊂ support of the QR idempotent
connection: The QR code of length p is defined by the QR set. ES₅ fails at p iff S₃(p) ⊆ QR. Coding theory studies which structured sets sit inside QR (e.g. minimum-weight words, automorphism group PSL₂(p) acting on QR codes).
why: The QR code's automorphism group PSL₂(F_p) is large. Words (as SL₂ data) act naturally, so S₃(p) ⊆ QR might be translated into a code-automorphism statement.
first_step: Check whether S₃(p) is a union of orbits of some subgroup of PSL₂(F_p) stabilising QR; if so, failure would be forced or forbidden group-theoretically.
refs: MacWilliams–Sloane, The Theory of Error-Correcting Codes, ch. 16

title: Gauss-sum / Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃(p)} at the quadratic character
connection: ES₅(p) ⇔ Σ_{A ∈ S₃(p)} (A/p) < |S₃(p)|. In coding/Fourier terms, the quadratic Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃} must not be maximal. Uncertainty principles (Tao's prime-field uncertainty, Biró–Meshulam) bound how concentrated a set and its Fourier transform can be.
why: Tao's uncertainty principle for F_p says |supp f| + |supp f̂| ≥ p + 1. Indicator sets that are subsets of QR have structured Fourier transforms, which gives a potential contradiction with S₃'s known Fourier structure.
first_step: Compute the Fourier transform of 1_{S₃(p)} for p < 5000; check whether 'S₃ ⊆ QR' would force a Fourier property contradicted by S₃'s divisor structure.
refs: Tao, An uncertainty principle for cyclic groups of prime order (MRL 2005)

title: Lindström–Gessel–Viennot: words as non-intersecting lattice path families with determinant tuv−u−v
connection: det M(t,u,v) can be read as a signed count of path systems in a planar network (LGV). If the planar network can be chosen so that the count is non-negative termwise, the cofactor A and its class get a path interpretation.
why: LGV gives combinatorial meaning to determinants and cofactors, the same objects as the ES sign (cofactor A mod p). Positivity of path counts is automatic.
first_step: Construct the planar network whose LGV matrix is M(t,u,v); interpret A = tu−1 as a path count and the slot-lemma 4-divisibility as a parity/symmetry of path families.

title: Slot lemma as a van der Blij / Gauss–Milgram formula for odd lattices (characteristic covectors)
connection: For an odd lattice, the Gauss sum of the discriminant form is governed by σ − w² mod 8, where w is a characteristic covector (van der Blij, Brown invariant). For the chain lattice, w has coordinates (v,t,u) mod 2 and w² has denominator p. This plausibly yields (A/p) as a function of p mod 8 and the parity pattern of (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1), i.e. the slot lemma.
why: It would give the slot lemma a structural (lattice-theoretic) proof and a generalisation to chains of any length, i.e. an exact sign rule for λ(p) ≤ L words.
first_step: Compute σ − w² mod 8 symbolically for the 3-chain and compare with the slot-lemma indicator over all parity classes of (t,u,v) mod 8; then do the 4-chain.
refs: van der Blij, An invariant of quadratic forms mod 8 (1959)

title: Stern's diatomic sequence: (p, A) = (s(k), s(k+1)) and HJ length as a binary-run statistic of k
connection: Every coprime pair occurs exactly once as consecutive Stern values, and the CF of p/A is encoded by the run lengths of k's binary expansion. ES₅ ⇔ some k with s(k) = p, s(k±1) ≡ non-residue, and k's binary word in a 3-run HJ pattern.
why: This makes ES₅ a statement about binary words, so automata/regular-language tools (automatic sequences, Stern's sequence is 2-regular) apply.
first_step: Find the exact HJ-run encoding (LORENZINI_W §7 has a Stern coding); enumerate k with ≤ 3 HJ-runs and s(k) = p, check the sign.

title: Hilbert basis of a 2-dimensional cone: ES₅ ⇔ a cone of index p in the non-residue class with a 5-element Hilbert basis
connection: The Hilbert basis of cone((0,1),(p,−A)) consists of the HJ convergents, so it has r(p/A) + 2 elements. ES₅ ⇔ some cone of type 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has Hilbert basis of size 5.
why: Integer-programming/commutative-algebra native: Hilbert-basis sizes and normal semigroup rings (embedding dimension). Toric-ideal theory gives explicit invariants.
first_step: Compute the semigroup-ring invariants (Hilbert series, a-invariant) of the 5-element cones and test whether the sign is a ring-theoretic invariant (e.g. class group element of the toric ring).

title: Hecke (Rosen) continued fractions: ES-type statements for Hecke triangle groups G_q
connection: Replace SL₂(ℤ) by the Hecke group G_q and HJ fractions by Rosen λ_q-fractions. 'Every element of a cusp set has a length-3 expansion with a character condition' becomes a family of ES-analogues indexed by q.
why: Some Hecke groups are arithmetic (q = 3, 4, 6) and others non-arithmetic. Comparing ES analogues across them separates arithmetic from combinatorial ingredients.
first_step: Define the λ₄-analogue (G₄ is commensurable with Γ₀(2)) of words and check whether a T1-type obstruction occurs.
refs: Rosen, A class of continued fractions associated with certain properly discontinuous groups (Duke 1954)

title: Integrable billiards / Sturmian cutting sequences of slope A/p in a square
connection: A billiard trajectory in the unit square with slope A/p has a cutting sequence (Sturmian/Christoffel word). HJ length is a renormalisation depth (number of Rauzy–Veech-type induction steps of a specific kind).
why: Rauzy–Veech induction is the dynamics-native renormalisation, and it has a version for square-tiled surfaces where arithmetic data (p) enters as the number of squares.
first_step: Identify HJ steps with a renormalisation algorithm on the square torus; check whether a square-tiled surface with p squares realises words as cylinder decompositions.

title: Transport laws as a semigroup action: ES failures form a set closed under 'inverse transport'
connection: ES(m) ⇒ ES(km) trivially, and the repo has transport laws between different n. The failure set F is downward-closed under divisibility (if ES(n) fails then ES(d) fails for all d | n). Order theory: F is an order ideal in (ℕ, |).
why: Order-ideal structure plus density-zero (Vaughan) gives constraints, e.g. F ∩ primes determines F. Translating richer transport laws into a semigroup acting on ℕ gives an algebraic object (orbit closures).
first_step: List all proved transport laws (TRANSPORT_LAW.md, DELTA_TRANSPORT.md) as maps n ↦ f(n). Compute the semigroup they generate and its orbits on primes ≤ 10⁶.

title: Torus bundles T_{γ_w}: H₁ order |tr γ_w − 2| and Anosov dynamics
connection: The mapping torus of γ_w on T² has H₁ = ℤ ⊕ coker(γ_w − I) with |coker| = |tr γ_w − 2| = tu + tv − 4. Its linking form and Sol geometry are explicit.
why: A 3-manifold carrier where the trace, not p, is the order. The ES sign may appear as a linking-form class at a different modulus, which gives a new dictionary for transport between p and traces.
first_step: Compute the linking form of T_{γ_w} for words at p < 300 and look for a relation between its square class and (A/p).

title: Mod-p relaxation: depth-3 products in SL₂(F_p) generated by M(b) and Helfgott growth
connection: Modulo p, tuv − u − v ≡ 0 allows words of kp for any k. In SL₂(F_p), the set X = {M(b) : b ∈ F_p} grows: X·X·X is large (Helfgott, Bourgain–Gamburd). This is the mod-p relaxation of ES₅ (losing the archimedean size condition).
why: It isolates the archimedean condition (tuv − u − v = p exactly) as the whole content, a sharp calibration: the algebraic mod-p problem is easy, and the size cut is hard.
first_step: Record the mod-p statement: for each p, does M(v)M(t)M(u) ≡ upper-triangular-with-sign have solutions with t,u,v small? Find the smallest letter bound needed vs p.
refs: Helfgott, Growth and generation in SL₂(ℤ/pℤ) (Ann. Math. 2008)

title: Integer matrices with prescribed characteristic polynomial: ES words as conjugacy classes
connection: Words correspond to γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with b = p and a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c). Counting SL₂(ℤ) matrices with given trace and a fixed entry is a classical problem (Eskin–McMullen counting in affine symmetric varieties).
why: Eskin–McMullen/Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak give asymptotic counts in growing balls, which shows the shape of the main term but with no fixed-p pointwise content (B3).
first_step: Note calibration; compute the count of γ with b = p and trace ≤ T as T grows, and its sign-weighted version.
refs: Eskin–McMullen, Mixing, counting, and equidistribution in Lie groups (Duke 1993)

title: Fourier–Dedekind sums / Beck–Robins: lattice points in the word region via Dedekind–Rademacher sums
connection: Counting lattice points in rational polytopes yields Fourier–Dedekind sums (Beck–Robins). The ES₅ sign involves Dedekind sums (DEDEKIND_ES). Combining the two might express Σ_{words} (sign) as a finite combination of Dedekind–Rademacher sums.
why: Dedekind–Rademacher sums satisfy reciprocity laws that allow fast evaluation and sometimes positivity statements.
first_step: Express |L₃(p)| and Σ (A/p) for p < 1000 in terms of Dedekind–Rademacher sums r_n(a,b;c) by linear fitting; look for exact identities.

title: Ehrhart theory for the word region: quasi-polynomial in p for fixed letters
connection: For a fixed letter t, the number of words of level t as a function of p is a divisor-type count, not a quasi-polynomial. Restricted to fixed (t,u), it is a periodic function of p (Ehrhart in 1D).
why: It explains exactly where the Ehrhart (polynomial) structure breaks: at the hyperbola. Native calibration.
first_step: Calibration only: write the counts and note the hyperbolic break.

title: Heilbronn's average CF length with a quadratic-character twist
connection: Heilbronn: the average number of steps of the Euclidean algorithm on a/p is (12 log 2/π²) log p. Twisting by (a/p), the difference between average lengths over QR and QNR a is a 'character-correlated CF statistic'.
why: If QNRs have systematically shorter/longer expansions (in HJ form), that is a global bias relevant to λ(p) ≤ 3. Twisted Heilbronn sums reduce to Kloosterman-type sums (Ustinov's methods).
first_step: Caveat from a cheap test (scripts/z52b_translate_cheap.py, p < 3000): the plain mean of HJ length is dominated by a near p (p/(p−1) = [[2,…,2]] has length p−1, and (−1/p) = 1 puts it in QR), so QR − QNR mean differences are large noise (0.2 to 9.7). Use regular-CF length, log-HJ length or the count of A with r(p/A) ≤ L instead, for p < 10⁵.
refs: Ustinov, on statistical properties of finite continued fractions (check)

title: Pell-like recurrence: words at p from words at smaller primes via SL₂ conjugation by a fixed matrix
connection: Conjugating γ_w by a fixed S ∈ SL₂(ℤ) preserves trace but moves the entry p to a new value b′ = linear in (a,b,c,d). Integer orbits of the conjugation action on {γ with b prime} are Pell-like recurrences relating words of different primes.
why: It gives transport laws with group structure (like Vieta jumping). If a recurrence preserves the sign and sizes, failures would propagate along orbits.
first_step: For S = [[1,1],[0,1]] and [[1,0],[1,1]], compute how words transform (when the image is a word) and how the sign changes.

title: Meta: the chain matrix M(t,u,v) as a common carrier in ≥ 8 fields — a transfer table of nearest theorems
connection: M(t,u,v) is simultaneously a reduced Laplacian, an electrical network, a ternary Gram matrix, a plumbing intersection form, a cyclic-quotient resolution graph, a FQH K-matrix, an A₂ frieze with coefficient and an SL₂ word. For each field, record the strongest pointwise existence theorem about this object.
why: It organises the translation work so that a single new theorem in one field can be checked for transfer to all others.
first_step: Build the table (field, object, nearest pointwise theorem, what it would need) from items in this lane; mark empty cells as targets.

title: Frobenius number analogue for three generators: n = tuv − u − v as a three-generator semigroup statistic?
connection: For coprime u, v, uv − u − v is the Frobenius number of ⟨u,v⟩. For three generators there are formulas (e.g. for ⟨u, v, w⟩ with structure, Rødseth). Is tuv − u − v the Frobenius number of a natural 3-generated semigroup (for instance ⟨u, v, tuv⟩ is trivial)? If so, I3 becomes 'every large n is a Frobenius number of a semigroup of a given shape'.
why: 'Which integers are Frobenius numbers of 3-generated semigroups' is a studied question; a match would bring that literature in.
first_step: Search small cases: for given n = tuv − u − v, compute Frobenius numbers of ⟨a,b,c⟩ with a,b,c ≤ 50 and test whether some natural family reproduces tuv − u − v.

title: Conjugacy classes in SL₂(ℤ/4) and the slot lemma: '4 divides a pentagon entry' as a class condition on γ_w mod 4
connection: The slot lemma is a mod-4 condition on (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1), i.e. on γ_w mod 4 together with the frieze. SL₂(ℤ/4) has order 48; the sign may be a class function on SL₂(ℤ/4) restricted to word images.
why: A class-function description would let representation theory of the finite group SL₂(ℤ/4) (and its Weil representation) organise all sign computations.
first_step: Tabulate γ_w mod 4 and mod 8 for all words of p < 10⁴; check whether the sign is a function of the conjugacy class (or of the double coset) mod 4 or 8.

title: Additive energy / multiplicative energy of the word set and character-sum bounds via energy
connection: Bounds for Σ_{A∈S} χ(A) over a set S follow from its multiplicative energy E(S) (Shkredov, Chang). S₃(p) is small (log²p), so energy bounds are trivial, but over the union ∪_{L ≤ L₀} S_L(p) the energy might be small enough.
why: It is the native additive-combinatorics route to non-trivial character sums over thin sets, and it pins down the minimal L where energy methods start working.
first_step: Compute the multiplicative energy of S_L(p) for L ≤ 6 and p ~ 10⁵; find the least L where E(S_L) ≪ |S_L|³/p^δ.

title: Global by-excess (HJ) tree of all length-3 pairs and the forest colouring
connection: The HJ algorithm acts on pairs: (p, A) → (A, u) → (u, 1) → (1, 0) for p/A = [[v,t,u]] (A = tu − 1, vA − p = u). Reading it backwards, all pairs (m, a) of HJ length 3, over all m, form level 3 of one global tree rooted at (1, 0) (a Stern–Brocot-type tree for the by-excess algorithm). Mod p, u ≡ vA, which recovers (A/p) = (uv/p), the forest colouring.
why: It places all words for all p in one tree, so that the ES₅ question 'level-3 node with first coordinate p and QNR colour' becomes a tree-colouring question across p. Tree statistics such as the number of level-3 nodes with first coordinate m (≍ log²m) are explicit.
first_step: Generate the level-3 layer of the global tree for m < 10⁶; for each prime m record the colours; look for inherited colour patterns from level-2 parents (u,1) → (tu−1, u) that are independent of m.

title: Integer-coefficient Ehrhart-type identity for the I3 count via negative continuants (Euler's continuant polynomials)
connection: Negative continuants K(b₁,…,b_k) are polynomials (Euler continuants with signs), and the I3/ES₅ word counts are counts of integer points on K = n. Euler's continuant identities (the 'Euler–Minding' rules) give transformations between continuants that might yield bijections between words of different n.
why: Continuant identities are exact. For length 3, K(v,t,u)K(t) − K(v,t)K(t,u) = −1 is exactly AA* = tp + 1 (checked). For longer words (the λ(p) ≤ L ladder), Euler–Minding identities give the analogous factorisations K(middle)·p + 1 = (left)(right), i.e. the level structure of length-L certificates.
first_step: Write the length-4 and length-5 analogues of AA* = tp + 1 via Euler–Minding (e.g. K(a,b,c,d)K(b,c) − K(a,b,c)K(b,c,d) = −1) and read off the 'level' and divisor-class condition for ES-type certificates at length L.

title: Continued-fraction periodicity vs. ES₅ length: Lagrange's proof structure
connection: Pell's solution comes from the periodic CF of √D. ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3 (a continued-fraction length condition for rationals with denominator p). Look for a quadratic irrational (depending on p) whose CF period contains an ES₅ witness, so periodicity forces existence.
why: Odd but concrete: links ES₅'s CF-length formulation to the one every-n theorem driven by CF structure.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, compute the CF periods of √p, √(4p+1), (1+√p)/2 and check whether an ES₅ witness can be read off from convergents.

title: Product of three sets in SL₂(ℤ): ES words as A·T·A with entry p
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd/Helfgott growth makes products of a few sets fill SL₂(F_q). ES words p = tuv − u − v are length-3 'minus continuants': the (1,1) entry of M(u)M(t)M(v) with M(a) = [[a,−1],[1,0]]. ES ⟺ some product in A·T·A (with t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p)) has the right entry.
why: Places ES in the product-set/growth framework where 'every element' theorems exist (at least modulo q).
first_step: Check numerically how the (1,1)-entries of M(u)M(t)M(v), u,v,t ≤ X, distribute modulo small q and whether all residues are hit with the expected frequency (local), then compare with the archimedean count.

title: Modular-Zaremba + size control: words with (1,2)-entry ≡ 0 (mod p) and size < 2p
connection: Moshchevitin–Shkredov solve a modular Zaremba problem by growth in SL₂(F_p). ES words: length-3 minus-continuant products; require the relevant entry ≡ 0 (mod p) and bounded by 2p, forcing equality with p. Equidistribution mod p of entries of words of archimedean size ≤ p is the needed input.
why: Separates ES into a modular part (growth, potentially 'every p') and a size part (counting words in a box).
first_step: Numerically test equidistribution mod p of the entries of length-3 words with entries ≤ p (count ≈ p log p) for p ~ 10⁶; measure deviations at 0 mod p.

title: Track full Zaremba as ES's closest structural analogue
connection: Zaremba (bounded partial quotients for every q) is at density one (BK, Huang A=5) but not every q, like ES. Any 'every q' progress for some A (or for structured q like Niederreiter's prime powers) would show what kind of argument crosses that wall.
why: Shared obstruction profile: thin semigroup, polylog-to-power main terms, density-one results.
first_step: Search for post-2020 Zaremba results ('Zaremba conjecture every denominator', Kan, Frolenkov, Shkredov, 2023–2026) and record whether any is 'every q' for some A.

title: Profinite Furstenberg: closed ×k-invariant subsets of Ẑ and the ES-hard set
connection: Furstenberg: every infinite closed ×2,×3-invariant subset of the circle is everything. ES certificate existence is closed under n → kn; the closure in Ẑ (or in the solenoid) of the 'certificate-free' set is invariant under division by units? Formulate the right dynamical system on Ẑ and classify its closed invariant sets.
why: Odd: a topological rigidity statement on Ẑ could say the profinite hard set is exactly the squares, which is the B1 picture.
first_step: Write down the action (ℤ_{>0}, ×) on Ẑ and determine which closed invariant subsets contain the profinite square-mimicking points.

title: Monotone-quantity flow on certificate space
connection: Perelman finished Poincaré with a flow and monotone entropy that forces termination at a canonical object. ES: define a deterministic 'flow' on candidate triples (x, y, z) for 4/p (e.g. a descent on the defect 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) using local moves) with a monovariant that can only stop at a certificate, and prove no other stopping states exist (or classify them).
why: Odd but concrete: a local-move dynamical system on integer triples is easy to experiment with; classification of its sinks is a finite-ish problem per p.
first_step: Design local moves (change one coordinate by ±1, or by divisor-jumps) decreasing |defect| and compute sinks for p ≤ 10⁴.
refs: arXiv:math/0211159 (Perelman, The entropy formula for the Ricci flow)

title: Frobenius count in SL₂(ℤ/q) for the SL₂ form of ES
connection: Ore-type proofs count solutions of word equations via Σ_χ χ(g)/χ(1). The SL₂ form asks for γ = [[a, p],[c, d]] with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c); reduced mod q this is a count of elements in a double-coset-type subset of SL₂(ℤ/q); its character expansion has nontrivial terms bounded by 1/χ(1) ~ 1/q.
why: Shows how much cancellation is available 'for free' in a nonabelian encoding (local information only, but with strong decay).
first_step: Compute for primes q the number of solutions mod q via characters of SL₂(F_q) and compare with the abelian (genus) expansion's error.
refs: Liebeck-O'Brien-Shalev-Tiep, The Ore conjecture, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 12 (2010) 939-1008

title: Wielandt-style orbit counting: a group action whose non-certificate orbits have size ≡ 0 (mod m)
connection: Wielandt proves Sylow existence because |X| = C(p^a m, p^a) ≢ 0 (mod p), so some orbit has size prime to p. ES: find a finite set X_p (e.g. 4-term or 'imprimitive' representations, or divisor configurations) with a group G (ℤ/3 permuting coordinates, S₃, or a dihedral group of moves) acting so that every orbit not containing a certificate has size divisible by m while |X_p| ≢ 0 (mod m).
why: Generalises the Zagier involution (m = 2) to larger groups where the needed congruence of |X_p| may be easier to establish.
first_step: Enumerate candidate (X_p, G) pairs for small p and check orbit-size divisibility; look for one where |X_p| mod m is given by a formula in p.

title: Unipotent flows and ES words: the horocycle parametrisation of minus-continuants
connection: Margulis used unipotent orbits. The matrices M(t) = [[t, −1],[1, 0]] are products of a unipotent [[1, t],[0, 1]] and a fixed rotation, so ES words M(u)M(t)M(v) are points on products of horocycle segments. Read ES as a statement about a three-step 'unipotent walk' hitting a target integer matrix.
why: Puts ES words into the language of unipotent dynamics, where every-orbit statements exist.
first_step: Write M(u)M(t)M(v) = n(u) w n(t) w n(v) w and characterise which targets [[p, ·],[·,·]] are reachable with t ∈ 4ℤ; compare with horospherical equidistribution scales.

title: Non-lacunary semigroups of levels: multiplicative closure of 'working levels'
connection: Furstenberg's ×2×3 rigidity uses non-lacunarity of {2^a 3^b}. If level C works for p, does level C·k work for p for many k? (If d | 4Cp + 1 with d ≡ −1 mod 4C, then nothing obvious at level Ck.) Study whether the set of working levels for p is close to a multiplicative semigroup.
why: If working levels had semigroup structure, rigidity theorems for multiplicative semigroups could constrain failure.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁷ compute the set of working levels and test closure under multiplication by small k.

title: Thin-semigroup local-global with the ES constraint t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p): local obstructions?
connection: Bourgain–Kontorovich require knowing the local (congruence) obstructions of the semigroup before counting. Compute the reductions mod q of the ES-word set with the constraint on t (4ℤ for one branch, 8ℤ − p for the other, which depends on p!) and determine exactly which residues of p are locally admissible; check that only squares-related obstructions appear (T1-type).
why: The p-dependent constraint (8ℤ − p) is unusual for thin-orbit theory; its local analysis is a concrete, finite task.
first_step: For q ≤ 200 compute the set of p mod q (and mod 8q) hit by words with each constraint branch.

title: Egyptian fractions on topological groups (Ross): ES in the circle group or in Q_p
connection: Ross extends structure results on sets of Egyptian fractions to subsets of topological groups. An ES analogue in R/Z or Q_p asks which elements are 3-term sums from a discrete generating set.
why: Topological closures of the set of 3-term sums (accumulation points are 2-term sums, etc.) give a 'derived set' picture; ES points must avoid being only limit points.
first_step: Read arXiv:2410.24165 to see which structure theorems carry over and whether derived-set orders give constraints on 4/n.

title: Riemann–Hurwitz integrality: a surface subgroup of Δ(x,y,z) of index d needs n | d(n − 4)
connection: For an ES solution, a torsion-free normal subgroup of index d in Δ(x,y,z) yields genus g with 2g − 2 = d(1 − 4/n). Hence n must divide d(n − 4); for prime n ≥ 5 this forces n | d.
why: Translates ES into 'Δ(x,y,z) has a finite quotient of order divisible by n with x, y, z element orders' — a group-theoretic existence statement where e.g. PSL₂(F_q) quotients (Macbeath) are classified.
first_step: For small n list ES triples and check whether PSL₂(F_p) is a quotient of Δ(x,y,z) (Macbeath's criterion); see if a uniform choice like PSL₂(F_p) suggests a construction.

title: Brieskorn links: ES solutions never give integral homology spheres
connection: The link of x^a + y^b + z^c is an integral homology sphere iff a, b, c are pairwise coprime. Pairwise coprime ES solutions are impossible (constraint-world item), so ES links always have non-trivial H₁.
why: Gives a topological invariant (H₁ of the link, related to gcds of the denominators) attached to every solution; the gcd skeleton of Type I/II solutions becomes the torsion of H₁.
first_step: Compute H₁ of Brieskorn links for ES triples of small p and compare with the Type I/II parameters.
